and artificial intelligence (AI) has been centered on understanding intelligence. Despite AI's progress, a comprehensive definition of intelligence remains elusive. Focusing exclusively on solving mathematical problems may stifle AI development, as it disregards key human intellectual capabilities, such as processing multimedia information, drawing conclusions based on reasoning, and learning through experience. Diverging from traditional computationally based AI, this study proposes a new direction for intelligence measurement, grounded in information theory's mutual information framework. This approach leverages symmetric kernel based mutual information to assess the similarity in content and semantics within probabilistic space. By showcasing its effectiveness, we test this method on both mathematical problem-solving AI and human participants, and provide initial evidence of the relevance of mutual information to both monolithic and multi-modal intelligence assessments. Additionally, this method's potential for evaluating AI algorithms processing multimedia information, such as those employing deep learning technologies, is demonstrated through assessment of its accuracy in evaluating object recognition tasks in four visual scenarios. Crucially, all assessments in this study are conducted holistically, reflecting the integrated structure of human intelligence. In the AI domain, a novel evaluation method is presented, analyzing the pruning and sparse structure of neural networks based on the theoretical model of intelligent agents. Finally, this study proposes a new structure for multi-modal intelligence based on the analytical model of human cognition, providing a framework for the analysis and design of AI systems. These AI systems are then evaluated and compared with human participants in terms of their performance on mathematical, multimedia, and learning tasks. Notably, both human participants and neural networks consisting of layered perceptrons exhibit similar capabilities across the three types of tasks. Although both human and AI share similarities in their performance patterns, the underlying explanations for their successes are distinct. Human participants perform well on these tasks through retention of relevant information, whereas neural networks achieve success through explicit multiplication of input variables. However, this study proposes a new design for multi-modal intelligence based on the analytical model of human cognition, emphasizing the importance of shared Latent Space knowledge. In conclusion, a new computational model for shared Latent Space knowledge, referred to as KS2, is developed and demonstrated through assessment and evaluation of neural networks consisting of layered perceptrons, and provided with implementation details and codes in Appendices A-D. Furthermore, a new computational model for intelligence is defined by referring to the shared Latent Space knowledge as a common baseline for representing joint variables. Each communication session is initiated by determining an $i$-th pair's sender and receiver ($1 \le i \le M$), with the sender engaging in a sub-activity and the receiver awaiting a specific sub-activity completion. A station involved in a sub-activity can concurrently initiate one communication session, with the sender choosing a random destination and the receiver specifying a single recipient. To facilitate concurrent sessions, a station can simultaneously start multiple connections with the sender contributing quantum key exchange through a blind session key using the benefits of two-way QKE. We also show the feasibility of module sharing and partial entanglement usage in two-way QKE. A recent advancement in computational tensor properties discovery has been made possible by using data-driven and machine learning techniques. These methods are utilized to simulate and analyze ESR spectra more efficiently. In this review, we discuss how these advancements are integrated into a computational framework to facilitate indirect measurements of molecular reactivity through ESR spectroscopy. A key aspect of this framework is its ability to accurately predict key molecular properties using data-driven and machine learning approaches. Preliminary results from the application of this framework demonstrate its potential in making accurate predictions about molecular reactivity through a correlation with BESII spectroscopy data. However, more comprehensive studies are required to validate this approach and explore further opportunities for applying this framework to provide insights into reactivity through BESII spectroscopy analysis. A Python package named molcaser is introduced as a demonstration of the computational framework. A related package named tensorknowledge, which is utilized in molcaser, is also introduced as a resource for computing molecular tensor properties. Both packages are currently in an early version and are expected to undergo significant development in the future. A collaborative approach is proposed to involve experimental measurements of ESR spectra to provide insights into molecular structure. A discussion on potential implications of using machine learning to guide ESR simulations is also provided, focusing on the importance of providing uncertainty estimates and restricting model use to its designated domain to minimize overfitting. A connection to quasi-classical approximation is demonstrated for a key molecular property but remains an area of ongoing research. A related outcome involving O(3) symmetry is explored as another potential application of data-driven and machine learning approaches to guide ESR simulations. A summary of key findings and a demonstration of the computational framework, along with recommendations for future development, are provided in the conclusion. Causes of imbalanced learning for binary classification tasks in the context of molecular optimization are also identified and potential remedies are suggested. A review of contemporary optimization techniques is provided as a contrast to the machine learning-based approach to molecular optimization, and a related critique of the application of gradient descent to atomistic parameters is provided. A discussion on the differential impact of uncertainty estimation and overfitting on molecular optimization is also provided, along with recommendations for rectifying imbalanced data and minimizing the risk of extrapolation. A review of the application of regularization, total variational loss, and thresholding to mitigate the problem of overfitting in the context of molecular optimization is provided. disease progression and Age-dependent Co-variance in Early-stage Markov models for Prostate Cancer, applying Bayesian methods. Prostate cancer development is highly dependent on patient age due to various biological and clinical factors. This research estimates age-specific probabilities of having one or more cancers and facilitates comparison with a common benchmark used for prostate cancer screening assessments. To facilitate transparent and comprehensive analysis, all computation codes and data sources have been made publicly accessible. However, simulation-based studies are required to evaluate our proposed model's performance in predicting patient states, particularly since there is limited access to detailed individual disease progression data. To address this limitation, we conducted a real-world study and compared our model's predictions with patient diagnosis and treatment records, demonstrating that jointly estimating age-specific disease progression and co-variance is feasible and yields more accurate outcomes. In its current application, the model primarily focuses on accurately estimating the mean and variance of a patient's early-stage prostate cancer characteristics given their age. Ultimately, the jointly estimated disease progression and co-variance will be key components in developing a Prostate Cancer Growth Model. This model will serve as the foundation for integrating it into the NCI's E-Cytoplasm Agency to support individualized treatment decisions within clinical trials. Furthermore, the model will enable researchers to evaluate the risk-benefit profiles of different treatment strategies and investigate non-malignant health outcomes associated with specific interventions. Additionally, the model will allow for an assessment of the potential consequences of variations in prostate cancer diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring procedures on patient health outcomes and numbers affected. Once fully integrated with other Agency members, the model will support comprehensive investigation of systems-level interventions. All simulation-related materials have been made accessible at: https://github.com/joemichler/PCCVM/tree/model-2022. Although single-layer graphene exhibits unique electrical properties, it also exhibits mechanical instability and is prone to rolling up into a two-dimensional structure.  By controlling curvature, researchers have been able to naturally create nanoscale devices with spin-based properties from graphene.  Recent studies involving curvature-sensitive graphene have focused on van der Waals layers, but our work presents a new approach using bending a single graphene layer and leveraging its inherent two-dimensional characteristics.  We used molecular dynamics simulations via the MARTINI model to simulate various graphene configurations when subjected to different bending pressures and temperatures.  Our results show that incorporating a layer of water on one side of graphene can induce a transition to a hexagonal structure and create a nanoscale electronic device with spin properties when subjected to specific conditions.  Additionally, we found that bending pressures of up to 4 kBar and temperatures around 300K can stabilize a layer of water on one side of graphene and prevent its interaction with the other side.  Furthermore, we discovered that device thickness can be controlled through the arrangement of ions and water molecules, allowing for optimal device performance with a thickness of around 20 Angstroms.  Our study on bending a single graphene layer offers an innovative approach to creating nanoscale electronic devices with spin properties using two-dimensional materials and showcases their vast potential in design and functions.  Finally, we suggest a new set of names based on atomic operations to describe the nanoscale electronic devices with spin properties, ranging from DEW0 to DEW9.  Moreover, we found that bending graphene is compatible with our previous concept of TAEs and enables various applications such as attaching DNA, proteins or functionalized nanotubes to a graphene device via molecular bonding with the surface functional groups.  Finally, we conducted a quantitative assessment of our new concept in terms of its stability, flexibility and effectiveness with a specified set of bending pressures and temperatures and found that its effectiveness is comparable to other types of graphene devices with the surface functional groups.  However, we propose an improved design of the nanoscale electronic device with the surface functional groups, called DEW8, which can provide enhanced functionality and compatibility with TAEs at the cost of a slight reduction in its electronic transport properties.  Finally, we suggest a new type of graphene device, called DES0, which can provide additional functionality and compatibility with TAEs and TAEs-modified nanotubes or proteins at the cost of a significant reduction in its electronic transport properties

SPS) or single-photon addition (SPA) refers to a photonic device operation where an input photon is either added to or subtracted from a stored multi-photon quantum state, effecting either the elimination or increment of a photon number parity. SPS and SPA are indispensable in photonic research and applications such as Bell measurements, as they are mandatory operations, but have thus far proved to be challenging to realize in bulk photonic systems. Our work resolves this issue by developing a time-multiplexed technique that allows these operations to be performed, and we apply this method to realize the difference operator using a two-mode interferent system. Furthermore, we successfully implement the operator using a photonic chip containing two coupled resonators. Our results show that by employing $80$ optical taps and $80$ (un)coupling events, the error in parity measurement can be confined to less than $3\%$. Unlike previous methods relying on a truncation of Fock space, our time-multiplexed approach allows the parity measurement to be carried out across any desired photon number with a minimum of scattered light. Our scheme makes it possible to perform quantum algorithms and communicate via maximally entangled states, both critical in photonic research, to be executed more efficiently. It visually demonstrates and mathematically proves that implementing a Permutation Network through the in-place CX circuit and a linear initial qubit state leads to an equal overall cost as utilizing a universal two-qubit gate. Furthermore, it is shown that this Permutation Network can be used in Shor's algorithm, specifically in the final measurement phase, and that using this modulated approach yields the same resource requirements as Shor's original protocol. Unlike Shor's protocol, which requires O(log(N)) CX gates for a specific permutation but an inefficient SWAP gate for another, the Permutation Network allows for the efficient application of any permutation with a linear number of CX gates. It is also shown that this linear permutation can be used to obtain an almost optimal sample complexity for Shor's test of quantum computability under a different computational model. In addition to Permutation Networks, a new optical module for Shor's algorithm has been designed, which utilizes a specific linear permutation to reduce the number of required Bell pairs from O(log(N)) to O(sqrt(N)), and the article provides a description of the construction method. As a result, Shor's algorithm with this new modular component exhibits an improved resource complexity, with a reduced number of required Bell pairs and 10 less photons, compared to the original protocol. It is also shown that this modified Shor's algorithm can pass a strengthened version of the original computationally complex test. Lastly, some potential future applications of Permutation Networks in quantum algorithms are discussed, including the possibility of replacing costly permutations with them, and the potential to improve the efficiency of Shor's test of quantum computability using multiple Permutation Networks. Original contributions in this work involve Shor's algorithm's parallelized final measurement phase, modified to yield comparable complexity to the original protocol, and the substitution of Bell pair generation with a linear permutation, resulting in an improved complexity for both Shor's algorithm and the original test. Additionally, the applicability of Permutation Networks in quantum algorithms has been explored for the first time in this work. It has provided new contributions including the capability to efficiently apply any permutation with CX gates from T(log(N)) to T(1) and add a linear number of ancilla qubits, and the potential for Shor's algorithm to achieve improved complexity with a multi-Permutation Network setup. ) is a process for deducing a set of probabilities related to potential outcomes of an unknown function, based solely on randomly sampled values. Unlike traditional rule-based systems, PLD operates through probabilistic reasoning. The development of PLD, utilizing a combinatorial approach to analyzing polynomial equations, has led to several key contributions: PLD can determine the completeness of sets of probabilities; determine when a probability distribution is unique; develop an algorithm for inferring a probability distribution from sampled data; and provide an efficient logical framework for representing and working with probability distributions. The PLD method is demonstrated to be effective for identifying unique probability distributions of small dimensions, but may encounter limitations with regards to uniqueness determination in higher dimensions. The PLD method is presented as a combinatorial approach to analyzing polynomial equations, specifically focusing on monotone polynomials. The method has potential for broad applications in machine learning and data analysis, but currently undergoes computational limitations, primarily due to a high computational requirement for solving the underlying combinatorial problem. The development of PLD is ongoing and continuously evolving, with potential future iterations incorporating learnable components, such as neural networks, to address existing limitations. The PLD method is implemented within an open-source Python package, `probLawDiscovery`, facilitating easy replication of the results and implementation. The PLD method is accompanied by a tutorial consisting of Jupyter Notebooks providing an introduction to its principles and applications, as well as a comprehensive dataset consisting of probability distributions. The PLD method is publicly implemented through an algorithm in a form suitable for porting to GPU hardware, with an estimated time complexity of O(n e^(n log n)) and a lower bound of 10^11 operations per second, assuming a fully optimized implementation. The development of PLD is continuously evolving, with an estimated additional 10 years required to fully develop the method, assuming regular progress. The PLD method is innovatively presented through a story, providing practical insights into its development and the challenges encountered during its creation. The PLD method is the subject of an accompanying patent, with a pending status at the time of writing. The PLD method is the foundation upon which a novel neural network architecture is presented, consisting of a probabilistic prior layer. The new architecture is implemented through a hybrid model, consisting of a hybrid model HP-LPD, combining the PLD method with a deep neural network. The implementation details are documented within an accompanying paper. The HP-LPD model is evaluated on a well-known dataset, providing comparative results with respect to unique samples,

The multi-target JPDA filter aims to calculate the probability distribution of target states conditioned on observation data, with the goal of maintaining a manageable computational complexity. The number of possible target states versus detection cell associations in observed data results in an exponentially growing number of terms that need to be efficiently managed within the probability distribution. The main aim of this paper is to introduce a novel JPDA filter that utilizes neural networks to bypass the complex computation of multi-target state probabilities. The proposed neural network-based JPDA filter is expected to significantly reduce the computational time required for each update, with the advantage of only necessitating the training of a single neural network for various target numbers. The paper will provide a detailed derivation of the proposed neural network-based JPDA filter and evaluate its performance by comparing it with the standard JPDA filter. The feasibility of using the proposed method for sequence prediction will also be assessed. The paper will support its methodology with performance assessment results, which demonstrate that the neural network-based JPDA filter yields a speedup of more than 200 times relative to the JPDA filter, with adequate tracking accuracy. Furthermore, the paper will investigate the scalability of the proposed method for long-term prediction. The results indicate that neural network-based JPDA filters exhibit adequate tracking performance relative to the JPDA filter, with the advantage of significantly reduced computational time in both target state estimation tasks. The paper presents a new neural network-based JPDA filter that utilizes neural networks to efficiently manage the probability distribution of multi-target state estimates conditioned on observation data, thereby significantly reducing computational time while maintaining adequate tracking accuracy. The proposed method has potential applications in neural network-based neural-sensor fusion, neural-robot perception, and related areas, with the advantage of being suitable for deployment on embedded neural network platforms. The paper provides a source code of the proposed method at https://github.com/xuxiang87/jpdafl. The study also found that neural network-based prediction exhibits a substantial decrease in tracking quality relative to estimation, with the result of insufficient in-out of distribution target data for training the neural network-based JPDA filter. The proposed method has potential for further improvement by the use of adversarial learning, with the aim of defending against sensing corruption. coding scheme is introduced for multiplexing multiple messages at the same transmission time. The proposed code incorporates a linear code tied to a Gaussian manifold and a random d-arithmetical code. The primary benefit of this encoded representation is the straightforward creation of a permutation invariant block-coding model. Through a simple analysis, maximum achievable multiplexing gain is demonstrated to be equal to $mg=\frac{m} {\log_2 (m)}$ for $m \ge 2$, which shows a direct relationship between multiplexed message quantities and logarithmic decrease. The study further investigates a maximum multiplexed rate for half-space Gaussian channels and shows that, with sufficiently long coders, a near-optimal rate is achieved from the information-theoretic optimal rate function. Moreover, numerical simulation results confirm and compare the theoretical performance properties of the suggested coding scheme.  The paper's ideas have also inspired the development of new coding schemes for other geometric manifolds, including the Laplace residual manifold and Vandermonde manifold.  It is worth noting that, unlike previous studies where coding schemes perform optimally only when channel equations remain unchanged, the suggested block-coding scheme remains effective even when there are residual errors between transmitted points and their corresponding received estimates.  As such, this encoded representation may be seen as a way to explicitly incorporate the effects of multiplicative noise in communication systems.  With the presence of multiplicative noise, the effects on communication systems are not simply random - the distance between transmitted points and their corresponding received estimates carries valuable information about channel conditions.  With this in mind, a new coding scheme for multiplexing purposes has been proposed, capitalizing on knowledge of this noise-correlated distortion.  As such, this encoded representation may be seen as a way to explicitly incorporate the effects of multiplicative noise in communication systems. In this paper, we explore the potential of using neural networks to adapt RNNs to specific tasks. A new RNN architecture, called Residual Rectifier Linear Unit (RRLU), is introduced, featuring a residual layer that enhances RNN performance while maintaining its properties. A modification to the RRLU, incorporating a Hyperbolic Tangent (HT) layer, further improves RNN performance and efficiency. In our experiments, RRLU and HT-RRLU are tested on tasks such as sentiment analysis, error correction, and summarization, demonstrating improved performance and RNN flexibility in adapting to these tasks. Notably, HT-RRLU is shown to achieve nearly identical performance to the expert-designed General RNN (GRNN) while significantly reducing model parameters and computational complexity. The RRLU and HT-RRLU models, including our test datasets and code, are publicly available for download. Our study demonstrates that neural networks can effectively adapt RNNs to various tasks, thus circumventing the limitations of traditional RNNs. In addition, the paper identifies potential areas of research for further investigation. According to our results, neural network adaptation of RNNs can improve performance by as much as 14.2, 9.1, and 6.1 in F1-score, BLEU-4, and F1-score, respectively. Moreover, the number of required parameters is reduced by 52-64, and computational complexity is contained within a 30% margin, when compared to the expert-designed GRNN. X-ray spectroscopy has been integral to understanding the production of intermediate mass elements within massive stars through various processes such as the $\alpha$-process and neutron-capture. Nevertheless, laboratory creation of these elements has been challenging, specifically within nitrogen to silicon mass range. Our investigation involves simulating laser-driven nuclear experiments to produce elements within this mass range. Our model combines computational hydrodynamic and nuclear reaction data to analyze the production of these elements. Our focus is on the role of neutron-to-proton ratio for the creation of intermediate mass elements between nitrogen and silicon through simultaneous neutron and proton emission driven by laser irradiation. Our study also examines the impact of initial conditions on this process using three different initial state setups. Our investigation provides insight into the conditions required for the creation of these elements through laser-driven compressional energy. Our selected laser parameters match those feasible with current X-ray laser technology, making our findings applicable for experimental realization. Our analysis also considers how to optimize laser and initial conditions for enhanced production of these elements. Our study demonstrates that with specific initial conditions, sufficient neutron-to-proton ratio can be achieved for the creation of intermediate mass elements. Our investigation provides a computational model for the production of these elements, which can be verified through upcoming experimental studies. Our study also examines the possibility of using these elements as tracers for the analysis of massive star nucleosynthesis and astrophysical processes. Our investigation provides a computational and physical understanding of this complex nuclear phenomenon. Our study demonstrates that by achieving the right conditions, it is feasible to produce these elements through laser-driven compressional energy. Our investigation shows that using initial material with low binding energy and increasing the laser duration can produce and maintain the required neutron-to-proton ratio for the creation of these elements. However, things become more intricate when dealing with graphs that are not uniform, i.e., their edges do not assign equal probabilities to their endpoints. This paper addresses such non-uniform graphs and defines a divergence measure to analyze them. For a matching to be feasible under this new analysis, the divergence must be low, and we establish an exact threshold for it in a specific class of graphs with n vertices and a degree of at least n/3 plus 1. By applying the soliton with non-zero momentum to a beam of longitudinal magnetic fields, we generate a Hall effect, resulting in solitons recirculating around the beam. As the soliton moves along the beam, it undergoes precession, and this soliton recirculation exhibits characteristics similar to the quantum Hall effect. Additionally, the soliton's in-plane spin precession can be used to modulate a directional optical emission, which we demonstrate in a theoretical-experimental framework. This concept may facilitate the development of a new type of spin-based and valley-based quantum devices. The soliton recirculation also provides an opportunity to study solitons pushing other solitons in an orderly fashion, which is reminiscent of Hall junctions. Another possibility is that the soliton can be trapped by magnetic flux modulations, thereby allowing soliton-based devices to be created, with the soliton acting as a submicron-scale quantum bridge. Solitons can also be used to modulate optical emission at different polarization states due to their ability to spin precess, which could be used to develop efficient and stable photodetectors. The solitons can be trapped by shaping the magnetic beam, which results in solitons that are in-phase with the beam's momentum being emissive at a specific polarization, and solitons that are out-of-phase with the beam's momentum being emissive at an orthogonal polarization. This photodetector concept is based on a new type of spin- and valley-based detection, which is difficult to replicate with charge currents as it involves degenerate spin and valley states acting as a perfect heat sink due to spin-valley scattering. The current research proposes the use of solitons to achieve this detection rather than relying on the symmetry of a superconducting device. Building on a previous approach that incorporated Hennessy-Miller models into Isabelle/HOL, we extend its applicability to prove the correctness of programs utilizing channels for asynchronous communication.  By adapting channel mechanisms to a logical framework, we incorporate both the sending and receiving of signals into the formal foundation, and then use the composition of Hennessy-Miller models, along with the application of fairness conditions, to establish the stepwise and alternating operation of threads and channels.  This new approach has been successfully integrated into Isabelle/HOL, allowing for the formal verification of correctness of programs subject to weak fairness via an enhanced set of logical rules.  By incorporating an asynchronous $\uccurly X$ operator, we have refined the initial approach to simultaneously accommodate the asynchronous nature of channels and the fairness conditions in the context of stepwise operation.  Moreover, we have innovatively applied the application of channels to prove the correctness of programs.  Specifically, we have successfully proven the equivalence of programs with and without $\uccurly X$ operator, and also proven the correctness of programs with nested calls to channels.  Moreover, we have formally proven the correctness of programs that asynchronously wait for input at most $n$ times, and finally, we have formally proven the correctness of programs that asynchronously wait for input indefinitely.  These achievements represent the first application of deductive verification to asynchronous programs with channels for input and output.  By incorporating the additional operators, we have successfully handled all the key features of concurrent programs.  This new approach has now seamlessly accommodates the crucial aspects of asynchronous programs with channels for input and output.  Moreover, we believe that the applicability of Hennessy-Miller models to input/output channels marks a significant contribution towards automating verification for real-world programmings, and this integration into Isabelle/HOL constitutes a notable achievement in both deductive verification and process algebra.  Moreover, we believe that providing a functional proof of equivalence constitutes a notable achievement in both deductive verification and process algebra.  Finally, we plan to further expand upon these achievements, and intend to deeply examine scenarios of timed input/output, and concurrently access a shared resource using mutexes in a future work.  Moreover, we intend to further integrate Isabelle/HOL with a compiler, and have access to low-level source code as input for formal verification.  Finally, we believe that achieving this goal will constitute a notable achievement in both deductive verification and process algebra.

Their observed IMFs are found to be consistent with a scalable Kroupa IMF depending on cluster mass. Specifically, our model suggests that the slope of the IMF will become flatter as the cluster mass increases. We predict that the IMF of globular clusters should have a slope of around -1.35, which falls within the observed range of -1.4 to -1.1. We also found that the selection of massive O-type stars can affect the determined IMF slope by up to 0.1. Furthermore, our study points out that the slope of the IMF in younger clusters ($\sim$ 5 Myr) may be affected by ongoing supernova feedback, which may need to be considered when calculating their star formation efficiencies. Overall, our study suggests that the IMF of unbound star clusters may be unique and cannot be represented by a single, mass-independent function. Nevertheless, their well-characterized mass functions make them valuable testbeds for complex astrophysical models. Finally, our compilation of O-type star formation rates in young clusters indicates that their rates may be influenced by merging processes and feedback-driven processes, which are correlated with the cluster's dynamical state. This is consistent with recent observations of directed star formation towards the surrounding gas in these structures. The overall picture implies that a significant portion of the overall star formation in these regions may be taking place within these clusters and will continue to do so until they reach an appropriate state of relaxation. Prior to achieving this state, their rates of star formation will continue to fluctuate, which may result in the unique phenomenon of 'bursty' star formation observed in numerous H II regions and young clusters. We look forward to seeing the results of future studies on this topic, which will necessarily require extensive use of high-precision data from advanced telescopes. Future

This paper rectifies this issue by employing a flexible K-fold cross validation to separate the dataset into training and validation sets. The results show that by adjusting the number of folds (e.g. from 2 to 10), these models can reach segmentation accuracy on the AI2THES dataset that was unattainable using the traditional split training and validation sets. To address this concern, we perform a meta-analysis on flexible K-fold cross validation's performance on multiple datasets, comparing the results to a more conventional approach that trains and validates using the entire dataset. The analysis shows that applying the K-fold cross validation to datasets like CamVid and Cityscapes yields higher segmentation accuracy than using the traditional split method. Conversely, using the traditional split method yields better results on the AI2THES dataset. This suggests that flexible K-fold cross validation should be used for datasets like Cityscakes and CamVid, but not for AI2THES. 

  To address the limitation of flexible K-fold cross validation on other datasets, we perform an in-depth analysis of its performance on multiple state-of-the-art state-of-the-art unsupervised semantic segmentation algorithms. The results show that applying K-fold cross validation to these algorithms yields to poor generalization when cross evaluated on 6 different benchmark datasets. However, we have discovered that a straightforward weighted average of the predictions generated by each fold using the same training and validation splits as have yielded state-of-the-art results on the benchmark datasets. This approach can be implemented using the equation Y_hat = 1/N * (sum from i=0 to N-1 of Y_hat_i) where Y_hat_i is predicted by fold i and N is the number of folds. Using terahertz data from the James Clark Maxwell Telescope, we observed TW Hya's disk and isolated a submillimeter continuum emission pattern. This allowed us to develop a detailed radial profile and determine various metrics that characterize the disk's structure. Our analysis indicates that the disk has a central temperature of approximately 15 Kelvin, with a surface density that adheres to a standard disk model, but one that deviates from Madhavan et al.'s (2007) revised version. Additionally, we found that the disk's radial density variation follows an inverted 'M' shape, with dust grains largely absent in the outer regions. This absence could be due to an extended, gas-only region surrounding the disk. This finding supports TW Hya being an exemplar of an active young star with an active accretion phase. Moreover, it may only be transitional, with our observations suggesting this could occur at ages as low as 10 million years. Finally, it was observed that the disk's millimeter-wave continuum emission exhibits polarization, with our modeling suggesting the presence of millimeter-sized dust grains aligned in a disk midplane with reduced polarization in the outer regions, or alternative options which require either grain sizes in a narrow range or an extended region of grain alignment. We demonstrate that the perturbed problem shares the same family of long time solutions as the corresponding planar, reduced problem. A nontrivial long time solution exists in the perturbed problem if and only if it does in the reduced problem. Importantly, this result does not depend on the specific perturbation. We then apply this finding to two particular gradient vector fields, yielding two unconditional theorems on the long time behavior of solutions in the perturbed problem. Furthermore, an example shows that the perturbation is indeed relatively small in practice. Assuming the force is small ensures our analysis for any initial condition. We also show that the perturbation does not affect the stability or instability of solutions to the reduced problem. Finally, we use the fact that the perturbed problem and reduced problem share the same long time solutions to investigate the related magnetic geodesic equation. We demonstrate that a long time solution to this equation may also be a long time solution to the corresponding Hamiltonian system. We focus on an example from astrophysics: a white dwarf in an evolving mass-loss environment. We show that the long time behavior in this case depends on whether the magnetic field is strong or weak. If the magnetic field is strong, the motion is largely confined to the magnetic surface and we prove that the perturbed equations have a global positive solution, which is also a long time solution to the corresponding Hamiltonian system. If the magnetic field is weak, the motion may escape and we prove that the perturbed equations have no long time solution unless a specific condition, called minimal energy, is met. In this context, the planar problem with minimal energy is obtained for both cases and we show that the perturbation does not affect the stability or instability of solutions to the reduced problem. We then apply the result to a binary system to investigate the effect of the gravitational wave on the long time behavior of solutions. For a circular orbit in a binary system, the perturbed two-body problem shares the same long time solution as the corresponding magnetic geodesic equation. We show that the gravitational wave may weaken or strengthen the stability or instability of solutions to the magnetic geodesic equation and weak or strong magnetic fields have distinct effects on the long time behavior of solutions: a strong magnetic field confines the motion and we prove that the perturbed magnetic geodesic equation has a global positive solution for this case. Our findings show that the present-day trend is a result of the galaxy's dynamic changes over its 13 billion year history. We discovered that the early metallicity and galactic radius are inversely related, indicating that the inner regions of the galaxy were more metallic than the outer regions. incorporating diversity into ML models, yet the subject remains contentious. Certain individuals, including prominent scholars, argue that the emphasis on fairness, diversity, and set-identifiable learning may unnecessarily complicate AI systems, potentially increasing their susceptibility to manipulation. This position, in contrast, suggests that the opposite may be true - that these techniques provide essential safeguards against manipulation. Inspired by philosophical debates on free will and moral responsibility, the argument proposes that the utility of these techniques lies not in their ability to produce just or equitable outcomes, but rather in their requirement for explicit human intervention. By making more precise, explicit, and reversible decisions within the model, we may not ensure fairness in the classical sense, but we do ensure that the model's predictions are more transparent and amenable to counterfactual analysis - a crucial requirement for responsible AI. As such, the distinction between utility and responsibility emerges as a dominant ethical concern in the ML domain.

observations by the Cassini spacecraft, a numerical model of the Saturnian ring system has been created, focusing on the processes that produce rings such as the F, G, and E-rings. This model's distribution of particles as a function of radius and altitude is determined by an evolutionary process that begins with the Moon of Saturn (Mars) and pre-existing circum Saturnian ring material. This calculation is facilitated through a series of spherical grid cells in a radial plane, with each cell spanning from the moon's surface to orbit and containing multiple particles. For each cell, the time it takes for a particle to become shepherded by the moon is calculated and modeled using a binary encounter interaction. This modeling approach demonstrates that Saturn's moons have a substantial impact on ring formation and that ring evolution is ongoing. However, this dynamic means that the rings are constantly changing. For instance, if a moon were to lose all its particles, new particles would be added to fill the gap. This model also predicts that shepherding by the moon Moon of Saturn (Mars) is the primary factor in maintaining the F, G, and E-rings, with particle distributions that are consistent with observations. This model's ring formation mechanism is an attractive explanation for satellite loss scenarios proposed for the Cassini Mission. It is also compatible with the moon's stable orbit and does not require any changes in the moon's mass or orbit, demonstrating that ring formation is an inherent consequence of moon-orbiting physics. uncertainty in AI comes from the fact that real-world world state information, necessary for deriving decisions, can be fuzzy and incomplete. General-purpose agents functioning in such uncertain environments need to make two types of inferences: first, agents need to learn their environment's conditions, and second, they need to make decisions based on the derived knowledge. Unfortunately, the current AI framework is inadequate, because it treats learning and decision-making as two separate processes that happen at different times (off-policy and on-policy learning), or forces to choose between pessimistic (robust) and optimistic methods that either produce robust results but are slow or produce optimistic bounds that are inaccurate. We introduce a groundbreaking and mathematically-sound agent that simultaneously considers the dual tasks of learning and decision-making in the presence of uncertainty. We thoroughly evaluate its performance with real-world datasets against other state-of-the-art algorithms. This work lays the groundwork for future research on developing agents capable of tackling complex, uncertain real-world problems. The increasing complexity of deep learning models demands a corresponding rise in computational power, and as a result, these models have traditionally been evaluated on a technical basis, with little consideration given to their visual interpretability. Nevertheless, as these models have surpassed human performance in most classification tasks, there is now a greater emphasis on visual understanding and the inherent ability of these models to convey meaningful visual information through their representation. The main focus of this paper is to investigate and measure the visual interpretability of these models by examining the complexity of their internal representations using information theory-based measures, such as entropy, mutual information, and information coordination. Through an in-depth analysis of a 16-layer ResNet on the ImageNet dataset, we are able to provide a comprehensive overview of the network's representation complexity, and based on this, we propose a new unified framework for measuring visual interpretability. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through a visual understanding experiment, and discuss potential limitations and applications of the method. In response, we have developed a method to securely match patient identities across different EHR databases by utilizing and aggregating the existing information in those databases, all while preserving the confidentiality of individual patients. The consensus mechanism is crucial in maintaining the integrity of the blockchain, and the majority of systems rely on asynchronous components. Previous research has established lower bounds for asynchronous consensus, and the last advancement in this field was achieved 35 years ago by Newey and Riley. Their findings indicated that, within asynchronous settings, at least t + 2 rounds are necessitated to guarantee consensus with at least a 2/3 probability of success, where t represents the number of faulty entities. Despite initial assumptions suggesting that this result should be unimprovable and representing the optimal solution, recent advancements in pseudo-randomness have led to the development of a new solution for asynchronous consensus, realized in this paper, that facilitates a 2t-round consensus protocol with a success probability of at least 2/3 in a setting where up to t faulty entities are present. an intricate mathematical challenge with far-reaching implications for understanding social evolution and making predictions about future trends. To address this challenge, we developed a comprehensive framework that translates societal values into a configurable multivariate statistical model. By measuring changes in this model over time, we can identify the impact of both ordinary cultural fluctuations and large-scale shifts in value systems. Utilizing our framework, we analyzed cultural values in Germany from 2006 to 2019 and discovered evidence of both types of changes. In particular, we found that the country's values have consistently moved towards a more individualistic and diverse orientation, while also becoming less tolerant of ambiguity. Moreover, we found that these changes cannot be fully explained by the influence of ordinary cultural fluctuations, suggesting a significant impact of large-scale shifts in value systems. An unexpected finding of our study was the apparent lack of influence of the European sovereign debt crisis on Germany's cultural values. In addition to our findings related to long-term cultural evolution, we also demonstrated the effectiveness of our framework for making short-term predictions of cultural trends. These predictions revealed an unusual resonance in Germany's cultural values in 2019 that strongly suggests a continued move towards more individualistic and diverse orientations, with particular implications for the country's long-standing emphasis on fairness and conformity. In contrast to these optimistic findings, we discovered a growing sense of moral relativism in Germany, which may have negative consequences in the long term. The applicability of our framework to the analysis of cultural values across different geographical regions, such as the United States, China, and India, remains to be verified in future research. However, our study provides a crucial methodological base for this type of investigation. Finally, we proposed a set of influential values that could characterize a society focused on human well-being, including a high priority on fairness over conformity. In conclusion, the cultural values framework offers a valuable tool for capturing the complex and diverse nature of human culture and understanding its intricate evolution over time. It iteratively divides the scene into smaller parts until reaching a threshold, using a representation of the scene that distinguishes between clusters and textures. The algorithm begins with an initial partitioning of the scene, then alternates between two steps: refining the coarser visual properties of the parts until they match certain criteria, and dividing the scene into smaller units based on their differences in shape and appearance. The resulting parts are then grouped into coarser categories, and a model representing the interaction between spatially nearby and dissimilar parts is learned. Experimental results show that HASHTAG surpasses previous methods, both its direct unsupervised counterparts and supervised benchmarks, on various datasets and metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate its ability to generalize to new classes within the same domain using partial data, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The algorithm's flexibility also allows for seamless extension to other domains, and we apply it successfully to semantic segmentation of van scenes and 3D scenes of humans during various activities. This framework encapsulates the diversity of physical processes within quantum theory and offers a concrete algorithmic basis for understanding quantum correlations among multiple systems. By employing orthogonal operators within stabilizer states and transformations, our approach provides a unified model for describing quantum phenomena, detecting correlations, and defining novel, non-local resources for quantum information theory. We demonstrate that this framework has the potential to offer a more cohesive and unified view of quantum correlation, ultimately facilitating further advancements in understanding correlations in quantum systems. and Palacios provided a characterization of Markovian mixtures of degree sequences in a recent paper. This paper extends their result to characterize mixtures of degree sequences that are stochastic but do not necessarily Markovian. Additionally, the extension includes an investigation of ergodic stationary degree sequences. These findings have significant implications in network modeling where ergodic stationary degree sequences can be generated from any probability distribution. This presents a more relaxed condition than the Markov property, enabling the creation of a wider range of degree sequences. The study defines what it means for a degree sequence to be ergodic and demonstrates that any ergodic stationary degree sequence can be obtained from a Markovian mixtures. Furthermore, the sequences are classified into those that can be obtained from mixtures of Markovian degree sequences and those that cannot, revealing a substantial set of ergodic stationary degree sequences that cannot be characterized through Markovian mixtures. The study manipulates the boundary of the ergodic region, previously defined by Garay-Avenda\~no and Palacios, to establish a new representation of ergodic stationary degree sequences. Crucially, the findings in this study are consistent with the findings of Ranjan and Cook, who in a separate study found that the vast majority of the ergodic stationary networks on eight or more nodes have degree sequences that cannot be Markovian. The study concludes by offering directions for investigating properties of mixtures of degree sequences that are both ergodic and stationary.  Garay-Avenda\~no and Palacios recently characterized Markovian mixtures of degree sequences. This paper extends their result to characterize mixtures of degree sequences that are not necessarily Markovian. Furthermore, the study investigates ergodic stationary degree sequences. The study explores the conditions under which a degree sequence can be obtained from a mixtures of degree sequences that are both ergodic and stationary. In contrast to the Markovian mixtures, the study finds that there is no straightforward characterization of the ergodic stationary mixtures. The study succeeds in characterizing the ergodic stationary degree sequences on three or four nodes. However, for five or more nodes, the study finds that the ergodic stationary degree sequences that can be characterized through a degree-dependent bound are limited to those that can also be characterized through Markovian mixtures. Initially used as a general framework, LMs have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in multiple NLP applications such as information retrieval, question answering, and others. 
The success of LMs can be attributed to several essential aspects including their pre-training objectives, training data, model architecture, and training procedures in combination. 
Despite their impressive performance, LMs are susceptible to various types of adversarial examples that can be generated through different techniques including query-based and word-based methods. 
Currently, research focused on detecting and mitigating the query-based attacks which do not necessarily include malicious words. 
On the other hand, word-based attacks involve malicious words within the query that can trigger significant changes in the model's output when substituted with alternative words. 
We propose a novel approach called MultiTask Decoder (MTD) to enhance the decoder's resilience against the word-based attack by simultaneously decoding the query and its perturbed counterparts. 
The proposed MTD has been implemented and evaluated on the two widely-used NLP adversarial attack evaluation benchmarks. 
Our results reveal a notable boost in accuracy (around 4% improvement) when compared with one of the most powerful LM-based model called BAIT-Riv.

agalactic radio sources, including Gigahertz Peak Spectra sources and Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars, remains a topic of ongoing debate.  While diffuse jet plasma can produce soft X-rays through synchrotron radiation and inverse Compton processes, observations of X-ray flares in these sources, including 4C+39.31, suggest that they often arise from compact jets or compact jets expanding into surrounding medium.  The X-ray flux in these events typically predicts the occurrence of radio flux variations several months in advance, allowing for the execution of radio observing programs aimed at capturing these predicted flux variations.  Previous studies, however, have demonstrated that detecting these variations can be challenging due to the limited quality of the X-ray data and the relatively low sensitivity of radio telescopes.  To improve detection rates and timing accuracy, future programs should comprise larger arrays of radio telescopes and better quality X-ray data, including faster response times in case of X-ray flares.  The goal of these programs is to increase the frequency of successful predictions from 13\% to at least 30%.  To achieve this, we present a new technique that utilizes the morphological differences between X-ray and radio images to identify the source region for future radio observing programs.  The goal of these programs, with improved timing and sensitivity, is the determination of the physical properties of jet plasma, surrounding medium, and ambient radiation densities through radio frequency interference mitigation, multi-wavelength monitoring, and data analysis.  The resulting data will be made publicly available for further analysis.  The improved radio observing programs will also enable the execution of dual-frequency programs to improve detection rates and timing accuracy for the detection of variable sources.  The goal of these programs, with improved detection rates and timing, is to increase our understanding of the physical processes occurring in these sources, specifically loaning the jet for the purpose of an X-ray probe and improving the precision of very long baseline interferometry, leading to a better understanding of the physical properties of gigahertz peak spectrum source jets.  Finally, we present a new radio spectrum model called J3048-2657, consisting of 23 bands spanning 320 MHz to 22 GHz.  The model will be used for follow-up observations and future research into extragalactic radio sources.  The resulting data will be made publicly available for further analysis.  The improved data will allow us to further study the physical properties of gigahertz peak spectrum source jets, particularly lending the jet for the purpose of an X-ray probe.

We explore whether these ideas hold true for Josephson junctions. By employing the Pruisken-Eckennig-Roeder method and confirming with self-consistent calculations, we demonstrate that the standard Fermi-GBSE for the bath's leads and a semi-classical treatment of the junction accurately account for transport and relaxation phenomena over a broad parameter space. Our analysis also reveals that, regardless of the disease's strength, the persistence of species A is contingent upon the total extinction of species B through a specific transition function. Conversely, the extinction of species A does not necessarily lead to the extinction of species B, indicating that a threshold exists at which point the disease triggers eventual extinction in species A, while simultaneously allowing species B to persist or grow in density. Therefore, the disease plays a double role, acting as a first-order effect for species A and a second-order effect for species B. Furthermore, the analysis highlights unique qualitative properties. In the confined environment, the average population of species A is bounded below by a specific transition function, while species B is bounded above by a Michaelis-Menten function. In the open environment, both species are bounded by corresponding curves from the first-order system of Euler's method. However, when the black hole's orientation varies, its effect on the disk's behavior is largely overridden by the viscous forces. Consequently, the disk's dynamics are largely determined by the interactions between the accretion disk and a disk consisting of the angular momentum of the black hole. This alternative approach for studying the dynamics of extreme mass ratio inspirals and the associated electromagnetic signals is called the electrohydrodynamic model (EHD). It has the advantage of simplifying the complex problem of the dynamic alignment of the black hole with its electric field, which requires further investigation. The EHD model offers the possibility of obtaining a general prediction for the duration of the lifetime of the black hole without aligning its angular momentum with its electric field. It also predicts that the lifetime of the black hole should increase in direct proportion to the third power of the mass of the companion object. It also reveals other characteristics of the electromagnetic signals and the dynamic extreme mass ratio inspirals produced by the EHD model, which can serve as distinguishing features in searching for these events. The EHD model also predicts that the companion object must possess a mass of at least three times the mass of the sun, which corresponds to its own accretion disk having a size of at least 70 times the radius of the innermost stable orbit of the black hole. This implies that the duration of the lifetime of the black hole should increase in direct proportion to the mass of the companion object. Given that the electric field aligns with the angular momentum of the black hole under specific conditions of the dynamic extreme mass ratio inspirals, it is possible to use the properties of the black hole to determine the characteristics of its electric field, which in turn allows for the determination of the properties of the surrounding disk. This is true for the case of the dynamic extreme mass ratio inspirals produced by the disk consisting of the angular momentum of the black hole and the electromagnetic properties of the accretion disk. The properties of the disk are reflected in the electromagnetic signals and therefore provide valuable information about the properties of the black hole and the surrounding disk. aims to improve a multi-agent system's performance by leveraging collective experience. Unlike reinforcement learning, which requires actions within the environment, LfO enables agents to improve without interacting with their surroundings as long as they receive relevant information. The field of LfO spans various domains including computer vision, automatic acquisition of knowledge, and robotics, and is particularly beneficial in tasks where collaboration between agents is crucial. The field's versatility presents a significant challenge, and one way to overcome this is by examining the fundamental principles of learning from others. In this work, we explore the basics of LfO through the lens of linear regression. By using a regression problem to understand the process of adapting models based on collective experience, we are able to identify essential features and illustrate how they are applied across different domains using examples. We also discuss the concrete benefits of implementing LfO in real-world scenarios and demonstrate how the fundamental principles of linear regression in the collective learning context can aid experts in designing and applying the method to various tasks and problems. Specifically, we establish the fact that the class includes certain interacting Bose-Fermi models on a square lattice with periodic boundary conditions. Our proof is based on the concept of reduced density matrices for fermions and employs a Lieb-Robinson theorem to quantify the relationship between their location and velocity. We show that the energy gap property is directly linked to the non-degeneracy of the Fermi system and the effectiveness of a bosonic zero-mode filter, which is imposed by removing boundary bosons and imposing particle number conservation. These simulations reveal a clear demonstration of the energy gap property in quantum systems consisting of mixed fermionic and bosonic components. A significant concern preventing its adoption is the potential decline in battery life. This research seeks to explore ways to minimize this effect by introducing a load management strategy for mmWave BSs aimed at mobile devices. First, an optimization problem is formulated to find the optimal energy distribution between radio front-ends and the processing unit. An algorithm based on the subgradient method is proposed to solve this problem. Initially, the algorithm assumes full access to a device's computational capacity, a realistic assumption given that mmWave devices possess relatively high processing power. To account for computation capacity uncertainty, a probabilistic model is presented, which is based on arm-based multi-armed bandits. A novel algorithm based on umbral averaging is proposed to adapt to varying computational capacities, and simulated results demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving extended mmWave communication duration and prolonged radio front-end and processing unit lifetimes. These extensions and prolongations are achieved through the proposed algorithm's ability to optimize energy distribution at low computational overhead costs. Moreover, the umbral averaging algorithm successfully adapts to the device's evolving computational capacity over time, further validating its utility. This research has potential applications for extending the lifespan of mobile mmWave BSs and achieving communication performance improvements. These outcomes are particularly beneficial in autonomous vehicles, where reliable and high-performance data transfer is critical in ensuring traffic safety. Additional studies are required to investigate the algorithm's robustness in the event of adversarial users and the potential security implications that may arise. This work has provided a solid foundation for successfully implementing mmWave-based communication in vehicular networks, thus paving the way for performing realistic evaluations of autonomous vehicle perception using mmWave BSs. Moreover, the introduction of the umbral averaging algorithm is a notable contribution to the field of stochastic online optimization, as its average time complexity is significantly lower compared to existing algorithms. This effectiveness makes the algorithm a valuable tool in addressing the online energy efficiency issues in mmWave BSs. Under the mean-field assumption, we find that a two-body interaction can lead to a dynamical phase transition similar to those seen in typical one-body Fermi systems, revealing a continuous phase transition characterized by a compression factor and self-energy metrics on the complex plane. We extend this notion to broader $n$-body interactions but find that only mean-field theories with relatively low orders ($k\le 2$) yield tractable solutions analytically. We demonstrate the applicability of these findings to one-dimensional spin-1/2 systems involving the hard-core dimer interaction and a three-body interaction governed by a symmetric cubic nonlinearity. We further analyze how a variation in these interactions affects the spatial extension of the system's half-gap modes and their decay rates. Crucially, we observe that as the half-gap mode's energy approaches zero, its spatial extent grows indefinitely only in the ideal two-body interaction scenario; however, the presence of higher-order interactions results in a finite area and counterintuitively introduces significant non-Perturbative corrections in what would otherwise be a well-studied one-body system. These findings hold potential for experimental verification in optical lattice settings. Moreover, we propose an experiment that aims to distinguish between a thermodynamic phase transition and a dynamical one by observing a type-I half-gap mode's emergence at zero frequency within the time-domain as an analogue of the system's compressibility peak in the thermodynamic regime. We suggest that this experiment could be performed using state-of-the-art technology. Finally, we outline unexplored avenues for further investigation, including (i) extending the model to account for the finite size of clusters or systems and (ii) investigating the emergence of topological features within this class of quantum spin models. As such models are still underexplored, a deeper understanding of their behavior could lead to significant scientific advancements. Finally, we note that these findings hold substantial first-principles predictive power, allowing researchers to make precise predictions regarding the dynamical phase transitions of various $s$-spin systems when provided with the spin coupling strength and the system's band structure as input. The approach involves translating measurements of electric fields inside a region of interest into an image of the permittivity inside that area. The proposed method overcomes limitations associated with multiplicative models by limiting the number of basis vectors for the permittivity term, while exploiting structure in the data through a sparse approximation. The scheme uses a duality-based optimization method to solve a related problem, with a convex approximation of the wave equation integral operator ensuring efficiency. The effectiveness of the approach is shown through simulations in two and three dimensions, with synthetic data from electrical impedance tomography, while its application to real tomographic data illustrates its practical utility. Notably, the method's performance improves as the sparsity of the permittivity vector increases, with high sparsity yielding results comparable to a method that assumes a precise permittivity model. However, given the synthetic data sets, further investigations are needed to assess the method's resilience to noise and its performance with real data sets requiring ill-posed problem reformulation. This path integral formulation enables the construction of exact solutions for certain potentials, essentially a generalized harmonic oscillator, even in cases where the direct integration of the equations of motion is unfeasible. This path integral approach also lends itself well to analyzing propagator eigenfunctions in these generalized oscillator potentials. Furthermore, we examine explicit solutions for specific benchmark potential cases. Notably, we explore the generalization of the well-known Legendre polynomial solution to a generalized Gaussian from the ordinary Gaussian, a generalized Airy function solution from the ordinary Airy function, and a set of coupled generalized Hermite polynomial solutions from the ordinary Hermite polynomial solutions. We also review an existing exact solution in the context of path integrals for a particular prepotential case and extend this to a generalized version. Lastly, we discuss some general observations on the generalization of the explicit solution construction and the generalization of the Morse potential to a generalized variable metric in the phase space, especially when the coupling parameter or coupling constants are non-zero. Adaptive Filter (TELAF) framework that enhances the performance of adaptive filter algorithms by incorporating auxiliary data related to its tracking error. The tracking error is utilized to update parameter adjustments which in turn affect the adaptive algorithm's operating point and its associated noise resistance characteristics. As a result, the error associated with the adaptive algorithm is minimised through learning based on tracking requirements. The proposed TELAF framework is versatile and can be applied to any adaptive algorithm without imposing significant computational overhead. The flexibility of the TELAF allows it to facilitate real-time parameter tuning and adaptive parameter control without compromising the real-time capabilities of the underlying adaptive algorithm. In addition, the TELAF framework promotes a collaborative learning approach where the tracking error is exchanged between the adaptive algorithm and an auxiliary network, enabling the training of neural network structures for enhanced performance. The potential of the TELAF framework is exemplified through its application in noise reduction tasks within audio streaming systems. The TELAF framework is demonstrated to improve the performance of popular adaptive algorithms such as Normalized Least Mean Squares (NLMS) and Complex Gradient Descent LMS (CGD-LMS) in various network configurations. The extracted features from the collaborative learning with TELAF are used to construct a deep neural network, which is shown to excel over standard baseline networks. A speech signal's entropy rate serves as this theoretical minimum bandwidth; however, due to the speech signal's non-stationary nature, its entropy rate fluctuates over time. The findings on entropy rate could also shed light on the inherent redundancy within human language, contributing to ongoing research on the inherent redundancy within speech. quantum circuits has become an essential research area. Circuit complexity, measured by the smallest number of circuits required to approximate a given function, is not the only important consideration. Another crucial aspect is the overlap complexity, which represents the smallest overlap achievable between a given function and a family of quantum circuits. Researchers, including themselves, previously explored overlap complexity as a potential bound for circuit complexity. However, these studies failed to yield significant results in previous works. In our current work, we introduce a new method to overcome this challenge and achieve nontrivial overlaps for a significant portion of quantum circuits. We begin by identifying circuits based on specific parameters and then determine overlaps based on these parameters. It is interesting to note that the circuits we selected happen to be optimization of certain Pauli decoy gate circuits used in key distribution protocols. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by showing its application in two distinct areas: evaluating the secrecy of quantum key distribution protocols and assessing the security of one-way quantum computation. Our results specifically reveal that the overlap complexity of $n$-qubit Clifford circuits is at most $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{2^n/n})$. Furthermore, our technique enabled us to derive a upper bound for the circuit complexity of one-way quantum computation, specifically $\tilde\Omega(2^{n^{3/4}})$, a first-of-its-kind lower bound in this domain. Moreover, our method allowed us to derive a upper bound for the secrecy of BB84 key distribution when applied with $O(n^{1/4})$ random decoy states. We extended this result to a more advanced scenario involving $n$-qudit key distribution using $O(n^{1/4})$ random decoy states and still achieve a comparable secrecy margin when compared to the traditional approach that involves $O(n)$ classical replays. Our results can be viewed as an confirmation that overlap complexity serves as an important bound for circuit complexity. In addition to this, our method has the added advantage of providing lower bounds for complexity classes containing quantum sampling and non-oblivious quantum sampling. Finally, our technique has been extended to derive a quantum lower bound for circuit complexity, specifically $\tilde\Omega(2^{n^{3/5}})$ in the quantum query model on classical data. We further extended this by obtaining a quantum lower bound for circuit complexity, specifically $\tilde\Omega(2^{n^{3/5}})$ in the quantum query model on classical data. Our approach enhances knowledge memorization through a straightforward technique that utilizes a memory buffer for past data, aiding model performance in online settings. Moreover, we develop a novel mechanism for controlling memory retrieval, ensuring the model's inductive bias doesn't negatively impact retrieval results. When combined with standard knowledge distillation methods, our proposed approach results in substantial improvements for MultiWOZ, a notoriously challenging benchmark for task-oriented dialogue in continual learning environments. Our experiments demonstrate that our method achieves significantly better accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art approaches, with gains of over 8% when measured across all online key metrics. The accompanying code is publicly available at: https://github.com/josh-bertram/continual-memorization.  We've also included a public replica of our code at: https://colab.github.io Amerikaner-continual-memorization-public-lb1014v3‌. We discovered that our method can further excel when combined with existing knowledge distillation approaches, but there are no existing methods that tackle task-oriented dialogue in continual learning settings. Therefore, our simplest model, which solely incorporates memorization, achieves a top-3 ranking for all online metrics in a recent benchmark challenge for dialogue models: the DialogSoft benchmark. The challenge aims to identify the most robust dialogue models against various attacks, and our method is surprisingly effective even without leveraging knowledge distillation techniques. The results of our experiments are documented at: https://josh-bertram.github.io/continual-memorization. We're currently exploring a novel approach to tackling the challenge, which we'll detail in a forthcoming paper.  We've developed a method for tackling the challenge, which involves leveraging our memory mechanism to enhance model robustness. Our method is called "Memory-driven Regularization" (MDR), and we've shown that it can outperform existing techniques, including dialguesparsity, while also addressing a critical flaw in the challenge benchmark. Specifically, the challenge previously had a critical flaw that allowed models to easily exploit and overfit to a small training set of human-labeled data, thanks to a common trick in which participants can label their own model's outputs to improve its performance. Our method is designed to tackle the challenge without relying on such tricks, and we've shown that it can achieve superior results compared to existing methods that do utilize such tricks. To clarify how atmospheric dynamics are influenced by the resolution of numerical models, we (i) distinguish free energy in a four-dimensional phase space and (ii) examine exponential exponential growth occurring outside this space. This analysis leads to a prediction that the rate of exponential sensitivity to initial conditions and model resolution will decrease as the complexity of the atmosphere increases. Specifically, we expect this rate to decrease when moving from low-resolution to high-resolution models. Furthermore, we anticipate that initial errors will be evenly distributed across the phase space and that final errors will be concentrated in regions of high activity. Notably, these predictions have been confirmed in our study based on data from the atmosphere and the atmosphere-ocean model. In fact, applying this approach to the atmosphere and the atmosphere-ocean model, we have found that final errors are concentrated in regions characterized by negative skewness within the phase space. Notably, these findings hold within the limit of baroclinic instability and deepen as we increase the complexity of the atmosphere, confirming our theoretical predictions. This study provides a theoretical understanding of unresolved predictions in numerical climate models and sets the stage for further research in this area. Specifically, we propose evaluating the feasibility of using local fluctuation dissipation relations to complement model resolution and mitigate the initial value problem. Ultimately, these findings have significant implications for the practical management of numerical climate models. In the framework of the Standard Model, this angle is defined by the ratio of the W and Z boson coupling constants. However, measuring it precisely using observables at electron-positron colliders is more complicated than initially assumed. One such observable, related to the cross section of four fermion processes at these colliders, has previously been used to set constraints on new physics. In this study, the influence of the polarized initial state on this cross section is investigated, and it is found that polarized collisions can serve as a direct probe of parity violation, allowing for independent measurements of the electroweak mixing angle and the Weinberg angle's polarization kernel, which accounts for the interaction of left- and right-handed initial state electrons and positrons.
