ography dataset, comprised of 52500 images from 1117 locations, is a significant advancement in ophthalmic imaging. Analyzing this dataset enables researchers to break down complex eye diseases into manageable, locally-specific components, facilitating more effective diagnosis and treatment. Due to its comprehensive content, we introduce novel tasks such as vascular detection and classification to cater to diverse research objectives. To address these challenges, we suggest a transparent and explainable solution relying on deep learning and statistical methods. To the best of our knowledge, this technique is the first to tackle locally-specific vascular detection and classification tasks. Using a combination of patch-level and local attention mechanisms, along with a Bayesian approach, we demonstrate superior performance in achieving accurate local labels and generating reliable uncertainty metrics for unreferenced images. These uncertainty values enable researchers to identify suitable training images and focus on more challenging data. Evaluations on the UWCTRA dataset showcase exceptional performance, and further analysis reveals the newly proposed method's effectiveness in detecting tiny vascular features and its resilience against external influences. Due to its open-source nature, the locally-specific deep Bayesian attention model can be flexibly tailored to various applications, and its source code is available on GitHub at the address given below. This work has the potential to expand into multiple application domains, and potential directions for expansion are outlined in the discussion section. To facilitate local-specific deep learning in medical imaging domains, we provide a comprehensive set of hyperparameters used in this study, and the UWCRA dataset is hosted on a public data sharing platform. We hope this study can serve as a pioneering example for tackling locally-specific deep learning challenges in medical imaging.

This fundamental question about quantum entanglement has long been answered for spin particles by introducing the spinful entanglement of formation as an metric. However, no similar answer exists for optical modes, which are the basis for another critical aspect of quantum connection. In this paper, we provide a definition for the entanglement of connection by linking it to a modified version of Wigner negativity and propose an optimization problem to calculate its amount. By examining a three-photon gate, we investigate how Wigner negativity changes over time and show the validity of our definition through analysis of both independent systems and real-world applications involving quantum memory. Our study indicates that Wigner negativity from our definition can be used to measure the entanglement of connection. Moreover, our model allows us to identify when Wigner negativity as a connection measure fails to provide a clear answer in complex scenarios. This failure mainly occurs either when the density matrix has a block diagonal structure or when the Wigner function has a zero-point despite being negative. This result indicates the necessity of introducing an ancillary system to assess the connection entanglement in such cases. This study amounts to be the first attempt for providing a definition for the entanglement of connection in the context of Wigner function. By providing an amount metric for the connection entanglement, our definition allows for a clear interpretation of Wigner negativity as a connection measure. In contrast to spin connection measures which are based on correlations, our definition is based on a negative Wigner function and proposes an optimization problem to calculate the connection entanglement amount. As the ability to create a Wigner function negativity is a fundamental aspect of quantum information processing, our definition is applicable to various protocols without any causal dependencies. In addition, our study can help to identify the practical feasibility of implementing these protocols by quantifying their connection entanglement using Wigner function negativity as an amount metric. This study can be considered an extension of earlier work on spin connection measures as it provides a definition for the entanglement of connection in terms of Wigner function negativity. In contrast to the earlier work on spin connection measures, our definition is based on Wigner function negativity which is more suitable for optical mode systems. This study is an attempt for providing a definition for the entanglement of connection in the context of Wigner function and as such, our proposal can help to advance our understanding of optical quantum communication by quantifying the connection entanglement amount using the proposed definition. The SEVERE is a event generator used to analyze and simulate strong interactions that occur when particles in final states undergo multiple quarks and gluons.  The program was originally written in FORTRAN and our Java conversion has also included the generation of C++ interfaces allowing the SEVERE code to be compiled from Java.  Our motivation for making this transition was to enhance the accessibility of event generators in theoretical particle physics by providing a modern multi-platform language that is widely adopted in both academia and industry.  In addition to describing our migration process, this report includes the outcome of this effort and suggests future directions for further integration of Java and C++.  In the course of our report, some universal guidelines for converting programming languages have also been mentioned.  Specifically, the FORTRAN to Java transition was carried out under limited resources and restrictive conditions.  Consequently, the experience from this project could serve as an example and reference for similar language conversions in the future.  By chance, a compiled version of the SEVERE code in Java is now available for download at no cost, providing the opportunity for students and professionals to practice their knowledge of particle physics by reproducing analyses that were previously presented at conferences.  A mobile application based on the SEVERE Java code has also been developed and submitted to the Google Play store.  In the application, users can 1) select a specific energy in GeV and 2) a specific final state made up of up, down, charm, and top quarks to analyze the distribution of particles in the program.  The analysis includes the generation of events, simulation of the energy in GeV, creation of background and signal events, and utilization of the SEVERE Java code to query generated data.  In addition to the translation from FORTRAN to Java, a C++ interface was implemented to maintain the performance of the SEVERE code.  Moreover, the introduction of Java and C++ has allowed the coupling of the SEVERE code to a number of other programs, including Monte Carlo generators, multivariate analysis, and detector simulations, all of which were previously in the FORTRAN of the SEVERE code.  A new version of the SEVERE code based on Java is now available for download at no cost and we are confident that the integration of Java and C++ has provided a highly versatile and efficient programming environment that has maintained the performance of the SEVERE code. This direct relationship offers the potential to influence the optical field's evolution over time through modulation, thereby providing an alternative means of managing light. Our study explores the possibility of modulating optical fields with multiple temporal periods in conjunction with their respective spectrally corresponding sidebands. We isolate and propagate the fields with distinct temporal periods by confining them to separate, temporal spatially varying regions within a nonlinear optical device. Specifically, we examine a setup comprising a cavity lined with a Kerr medium where the optical field's time period is modulated by a pump wave. Our analysis shows that the interference between the modulated fields with the unmodulated cavity photon results in a highly nonlinear and nonlinearizable dynamics. Our findings also highlight the formation of a self-organized system comprising interdependent temporal solitons. Moreover, we illustrate the transformation of these solitons and the emergence of another set of solitons with opposite phase relations. Ultimately, we demonstrate the emergence of a pairwise attractor dynamics where the temporal periods and amplitudes of the fields are interdependent and exhibit a nonlinear, localizable behavior. Our work yields new insights into the optical field's behavior and provides opportunities for developing innovative optical switching technologies using complex optical field manipulation. To mitigate these difficulties, a Gabor wavelet based approach for adaptive regularization of FWI has been developed, demonstrating the potential to overcome these limitations. The approach successfully determined the regularization parameters without user intervention, and significantly improved model recovery by reducing the need for extensive computational resources and user-tuned parameters.  The Gabor-based approach for adaptive regularization of FWI has significant implications for generalizations to Higher Order FWI(HFWI) and Multiscale FWI(MSWI).  The Gabor-based FWI algorithm has the potential to be widely generalized to HFWI and MSFWI because the approach does not rely on any user-tuned parameters that are often necessary for HFWI and MSFWI.  Furthermore, the Gabor-based algorithm for HFWI and MSFWI is currently being developed as part of an open-source model recovery code for FWI, 3D-MIRT-FWI, and SFWI, and will be made available via GitHub in the near future. Hypernetworks as a means of regularizing Deep Neural Networks.  Hypernetworks generate weights for primary networks on a per-sample basis, imposing structural constraints on their architecture.  Previous research has identified Hypernetworks as a viable regularization technique for shallow architectures.  Here, we investigate hypernetwork regularization for use with Deep Neural Networks, a area which has received relatively little attention.  Our paper presents the first empirical investigation of using Hypernetworks as regularization methods for very deep networks.  Interestingly, we find that Hypernetwork regularization leads to an alteration of the inductive bias of primary networks, causing them to favour features with larger spectra, thereby increasing their ability to generalize to new data.  Our results demonstrate that Hypernetwork regularization produces results on standard benchmarks which are comparable to those achieved using current leading regularization techniques.  Additionally, we provide analytical evidence that supports the use of Hypernetwork regularization as a means of promoting invariance in deep neural networks.  Our code is made available for public access at the address: \url{https://github.com/jase-clarkson/hypernetwork-regularization}.  Hypernetwork regularization has a wide range of potential applications, and could with further research, be a highly effective and generally applicable technique for analyzing deep neural networks.  As part of this study we carry out an in-depth analysis of Hypernetwork regularization in primary Cortical Networks, whose architecture is derived from their structural properties in biology.  Our findings suggest that Hypernetwork regularization is compatible with all types of Cortical Networks and can be applied during both their training and testing phases.  Moreover, we show that our analysis confirms the tendency of Hypernetworks to produce networks with spectrum-like features and, consequently, we are able to reproduce our empirical results from previous sections using our model.  Using our model, we are also able to better comprehend the effect of Hypernetwork regularization in altering the inductive bias of primary networks, revealing that Hypernetwork regularization leads to the emergence of invariance properties in deep neural networks to both translational and rotational transformations.  Our model is able to reproduce empirical results using Hypernetwork regularization and is therefore validated.  Our study using Hypernetwork regularization is the first analysis of a fundamental regularization technique for deep neural networks, and as our results demonstrate, Hypernetwork regularization is capable of promoting invariance in deep neural networks using principles from mathematical physics.  Moreover, Hypernetwork regularization is consistent with the principles of functional neuroscience, which is concerned with the functional analysis of the human brain. We aim to find the maximum trial count, denoted as $N$, such that the cumulative process retains a probabilistic (Bernoulli) distribution for each unique outcome. In other words, we seek the largest $N$ satisfying this condition for all possible outcome sets $\{\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_K\}$. To address this problem, we first explore the properties of the first two raw moment functions of the modified Bernoulli distribution, assuming $f_i(\xi_j)=\xi_j^{r_i}$, and show that the Bernoulli distribution limit exists and is unique for a sufficiently large $N$. Moreover, we uncover the required conditions for both the one-sided and two-sided moment bounds to hold, specifically the cross moments ${r_i \wedge r_j}$ for upper bounds and the maximum radii $\max_{i} r_i$ for lower bounds. To validate our theoretical analysis, we incorporate probability tools (central limit theorem and Berstein inequality) to establish the exact values of $N$ for small outcome sets $\{\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_K\}$. Finally, the performance of our proposed bound is illustrated through error simulation experiments. To streamline the presentation, the proof of our theoretical bound is presented in Supplement A. The deep learning-based approximation of the optimal trial count $N$ is discussed in Supplement B. Based on the results from both theoretical and experimental approaches, a numerical estimate for an infinite sequence of outcomes ($K\to\infty$) is obtained, resulting in a key conclusion: the cumulative process for all possible trial outcomes ($\xi_1=\xi_2=\cdots=\xi_K=1$ except one zero) converges to the Bernoulli distribution with $N$ equal to $K+1$. Furthermore, a general conjecture is presented about the properties of the weighted Bernoulli distribution. Specifically, if all radii $r_i$ are positive and the resulting cross moments ${r \wedge r_j}$ are sufficiently large for $K$ large, then the cumulative process converges to the weighted Bernoulli distribution. To verify this proposed conjecture, a series of numerical experiments are performed in the final section of the manuscript. Integration of roving game-camera data with capture-site information can provide comprehensive species coverage, bridging the gap between traditional capture-site data and 360{\deg} captures. This method is termed 'augmented capture-site data'. We believe this approach has the potential to enhance capture-site surveys and provide valuable additional information for species modelling, making it particularly beneficial for species such as the kiwi, whose 360-degree captures reveal high levels of activity at night. By integrating roving game-camera data with traditional capture-site information, we aim to demonstrate how augmented capture-site data can contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of species activity. This will be achieved by focusing on two species, the tokoeka (Apteryx australis) and the kiwi (Apteryx haastii). Results from the tokoeka show similar activity patterns on capture-sites and game-cameras, with the game-cameras capturing moderate activity on the capture-sites and revealing activity throughout the day as well as at night. Conversely, kiwi activity on capture-sites is the highest of all sites, including game-cameras, with a strong peak in activity at night as well as increased activity during summer. By incorporating roving game-camera data into traditional capture-site information, we aim to improve our understanding of kiwi activity patterns. However, further research is needed to identify factors that influence roving camera activity and trapping success before we can fully harness the potential of augmented capture-site data. Despite this limitation, we believe this approach can make valuable contributions to current conservation efforts and provide valuable additional information for species modelling. This research highlights the need for further investigation into using game-cameras as supplementary monitoring tools to enhance traditional capture-site information. Furthermore, we believe our method can be applied to a range of other bird species, including those such as the rare Hihi (Notiomys cedigus) and the Whinwhiri (Notiomys aliceae), for whom traditional capture-site information is limited due to low capture rates. Effective conservation and management of these species may depend on the successful use of augmented capture-site data. Finally, we recommend further research into using game-camera caged birds as supplementary conservation tools to inform enclosure design and management. This additional information can, in turn, contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of kiwi activity patterns on traditional capture-site information. Abstracting typical light-matter interactions through a quantum system's density matrix and a set of bosonic creators and annihilators, we explore how squeezing affects these systems.  By applying a specific squeezing transformation to these creators and annihilators, we derive the explicit time evolution of a density matrix under this transformed Hamiltonian.  Furthermore, we obtain the generalized squeezing relationships applicable to a broad class of bosonic systems including harmonic oscillators, optical cavities, and superconducting circuits.  We demonstrate that our findings can predict the outcomes of recent experiments with superconducting circuits and provide a simplified explanation for observed phenomena.  Additionally, we show how our model can be applied to a complex problem of optical cavity cooling, where we derive an analytic solution for the steady-state nonequilibrium system, consistent with prior experiments.  We anticipate that our analytical framework will contribute to understanding and interpreting the results of ongoing and future experiments.  We have made our work relevant by releasing a publicly accessible Python script (available at https://github.com/ajkozlov/ssquzee.git), enabling other researchers to reproduce our findings and explore additional applications.  Finally, by extending our model to fermionic systems, we identify squeezing a fermionic creator as a non-local coupling mechanism, where the strength of this coupling is determined by the square of the coherent amplitude. We suggest a quantum computing and drug discovery pipeline based on the molecular structure matching problem, and evaluate its performance using IBMQ's cloud-based quantum computing servers. With the pipeline's implementation in Python, which includes classical and quantum processing modules, we were able to achieve compilation times of around 30 milliseconds, input-output processing times of approximately 30 minutes, and optimal solution convergence within 30 seconds on IBMQ's 5-qubit chip. We also investigated the pipeline's scalability by testing it on the basis of the molecular structure matching problem using NCI1 dataset. Moreover, we found that the unique advantage of quantum computing lies in pattern recognition, which is particularly applicable to drug discovery, leading to promising outcomes, including the identification of potentially active molecules. We were able to enhance the accuracy of traditional machine learning models by incorporating quantum features and observed that the performance of our quantum-driven models exceeded that of their classical counterparts on the Delaunay diverse molecular pairs subdataset of NCI1. Lastly, by comparing the results obtained from quantum-inspired algorithms with those from actual quantum computers, we found a significant increase of up to 7% in accuracy in predicting the activity of molecules on the NCI1 dataset using the quantum-inspired K-Means algorithm. These experiments and findings illustrate the practical applicability of quantum computing and quantum-inspired algorithms to drug discovery and related problems, which are highly relevant to human health. These findings are particularly appealing because they show that quantum computing and quantum-inspired algorithms are contributing to an improvement in the precision of medical predictions, which has far-reaching implications for medical research and practice. The calculation of the total susceptible population, which determines the initial size of the outbreak, is also addressed in our research, which is particularly relevant for university campuses with public classes. In our analysis of data from two universities, we observe that the assumption of uniform transmission can result in a 50% overestimation of the actual transmission efficiency, which has a substantial impact on the calculation of the total susceptible population, which can lead to overestimation by more than 40%. Our work provides the foundation for re-evaluating historical data and conducting simultaneous transmission efficiency and susceptibility studies using targeted interventions on a larger scale, which may reveal a more accurate and alarming understanding of infectious diseases, which may in turn motivate the development of more effective control strategies and measures. However, we find that BNNs tend to overestimate their own uncertainty in relation to the outcome of their individual member networks. Inspired by the principle of maximum entropy, we present a neural network ensemble that minimizes its uncertainty in the general scenario and applies this formulation specifically when the outcome variables follow a Poisson distribution. The efficacy of our ensemble, particularly its uncertainty reduction, is demonstrated through both artificial experiments and real-world data analysis of RNA sequencing-based patient class labels. Comparing the precision of our method with that of BNNs, we notice a notable improvement in both the overall accuracy of predicting outcomes and the range of valid uncertainty. Additionally, our method contributes to the understanding of differential gene expression in various patient classes by providing valid uncertainty intervals for expression levels, which in turn facilitates a more transparent and reliable usage of RNA sequencing in clinical settings. The effectiveness of a black-box testing method in speeding up this process is evaluated based on two key factors: the benefits it offers over not conducting the test at all, and how efficiently it carries out the test.  The first factor is represented by the information gain of the method, while the second factor is represented by the accelerated running time, or AMC, associated with it.  A testing method's overall efficiency under a given testing framework is assessed through a metric that takes into account the method's information gain per unit of time, or IG/AMC.  A testing design is considered good if it leads to a method with high information value and running time efficiency.  However, the two factors are often disconnected: a method with high information value may actually run more slowly, and vice versa.  A testing design is considered good if it separates these factors.  The limits of these limits are known - if a method's information value and running time are connected by a logarithm - but the question remains open for hyperbolic limits, or exponential relationships between the two factors.  The next best thing is to analyze the other possible relationships between the two factors, such as quadratic, cubic, and other higher-order connections, and to identify testing designs that take advantage of these links.  The hyperbolic limit, where the method's running time increases according to a power function in relation to the information value it offers, is actually the highest possible limit for a testing design's efficiency - and indeed, this is the setup of the hyperbolic Monte Carlo method, or HMC.  The question then becomes whether this setup is the best possible limit for a testing design's efficiency.  A testing design is considered to be hyperbolic if it meets two key factors - that the method's running time increases according to a power function in relation to the information value it offers, and that the method's information value also increases according to a power function in relation to the number of samples.  The hyperbolic limit is the best possible limit for a testing design's efficiency if it meets these two factors, and the method's information value increases at a faster rate compared to the method's running time, or IG/AMC approaches infinity as the number of samples approaches infinity. scene representations using descriptive texts. The main goal is to assign meaningful attributes to scene elements based on written descriptions. To address this challenge, two novel tasks – attribute value prediction and attribute identification – are proposed. The former task involves inferring specific properties (e.g., size, color), whereas the latter entails identifying basic attributes (e.g., shape, texture). To accomplish these tasks, an interconnected network is required, capable of handling both tasks simultaneously. Drawing inspiration from existing visual recognition models, an extended network is proposed, integrating knowledge from both visual and language domains. The resulting model utilizes both visual and language inputs to produce a compact scene representation. To evaluate task effectiveness, two widely-used datasets (CUB-200-2011 and Stanford Car Dataset) are employed. To rectify a critical shortage of labeled data in this context, a novel self-supervised learning approach is developed. The model can seamlessly switch between its fully supervised, partially supervised, and fully unsupervised variants. The results of our model confirm its superiority over competing approaches within the attribute value prediction task, further demonstrating its capacity to identify attribute values in low-data settings. To bridge the gap between visual and language tasks, a unified latent space is achieved. Consequently, a model trained to recognize bird types can also recognize their descriptive attributes, such as bird sizes or colors. Moreover, when provided with a descriptive text describing a bird (e.g., large, green), the model can automatically infer the corresponding image content. To facilitate further research into visual-language attributes, two new datasets (Character Attributes and Kitchen Attributes) are introduced, focusing on identifying distinctive attributes of individuals (distinguished by hair color, age, etc.) and household items (defined by material, size, etc.). The results of our experiments from the top-performing models on these datasets are made available. The corresponding code and dataset models are presented in the supporting repositories. of a stable classical world is facilitated by a broad, artery-like distribution of entangled bonds between the environment and isolated systems.  The information contained within these bonds is readily available to observe, accounting for the apparent objective nature of reality.  The following investigation examines the origin of this widespread entanglement, focusing on its relationship with the bonds between systems and their surroundings, as well as with the information contained within observations.  The findings indicate that, during the initial stages of the arrow of time, a sort of feedback loop emerges: information becomes embedded in observations, leading to the clearing of entangled bonds, which in turn enables further observations to clear more extensively.  The connection between the clearing of entangled bonds and observations is shown to be responsible for the intrinsic objective nature of time.  The emergence of a stable classical world is thus attributed to a self-reinforcing process, beyond mere spontaneous occurrence.  The following analysis explores the foundational implications of this discovery, specifically its impact on the notion of reality as a whole and the role of observations within it.  The insights developed here are then applied, via a thought experiment, to address the measurement problem within Quantum Darwinism.  The experiment indicates that: (i) there is no genuine "collapse" of the superposition of states in a system observed interactively; (ii) although there is a genuine "collapse" in the case of systems not observed interactively, it can be explained by the environment's tendency to disentangle and to drift away from the system in question; (iii) finally, the distinction between the two instances of "collapse" lies in their respective time orientations, with the latter corresponding to the arrow of time inherent within classical reality.  Finally, the findings of this investigation are connected to the broader question of how matter came to possess momentum, and how momentum originated within the universe, revealing a connection between the two phenomena and a possible time-honored answer to the question.  Quantum Darwinism thus yields a natural, physical, and objective basis for the concept of reality as a whole, including the notion of observations clearing entangled bonds, and sheds light on the underlying basis of classical reality, including the arrow of time, the origin of momentum, and the emergence of a stable classical world. specific realizations of a more general recursive formula applicable to variational 
recursive models, including RNNs, ConvLSTM, and Transformer encoder models.
By expressing a forward pass through these models as a series of recurrent updates,

function that updates the recurrences at each time-step, while the overall 
recursive structure remains consistent.

involves applying the same recurrence in reverse order.

hardware, yielding significant performance boosts on platforms such as DNN-

recursive structure of these architectures is expected to facilitate their

For complex materials with multiple components, predicting the behaviour of individual constituents can be trivial, but their interaction and impact on each other is highly nonlinear. To tackle this complexity, a new method is presented using the multiplicative evolution of probability density functions, followed by a combination of the resulting outcomes. This method is restricted to independent changes in microstructures where the action of one component does not affect the others. Several applications are shown, such as the simplification of complex reactive systems, the use of partial information, and the calculation of the most critical parameters influencing phase transitions. This approach also allows for the integration of prior knowledge or observations, and its capability in tackling multiple independent parameters is significant for data-driven model construction. Several examples will demonstrate its value in the field of materials science. However, a major drawback of this approach is its restricted assumption of independent interactions, which may not always hold true. To overcome this limitation, a future research direction involving the consideration of interconnected microstructures is proposed. The method is put into practice by investigating the probability of material failure in brittle structures and by determining how the size of particles influences the fragmentation process of those particles. The method is found to produce accurate results, and they align with real experiments. Finally, a suggestion for future research is presented, involving the application of multiplicative methods to the calculation of the breakdown torque of fiber reinforced materials. This is particularly important in the field of composite materials and their failure mechanisms. The method is seen as a promising tool, and its straightforward approach makes it suitable for the integration of user-defined functions and experiments, promoting active user participation. At the same time, it is observed that the method is restricted to independent changes, which is not necessarily true in the field of materials science. Therefore, future research will focus on the development of a more comprehensive method that can capture both independent and interconnected microstructural changes. This will necessarily involve a higher level of complexity, and several possible approaches are presented to reduce this complexity as much as possible. win Schrödinger Institute's Number and Type challenge, which poses a universal deviation estimation problem for various mathematical domains. The task is to calculate the deviation in magnitude between a totally positive (non-negative) matrix and its closest approximation of a specific, lower-dimensional fully non-negative matrix. This problem applies to numerous fields such as computer science, signal processing, and physics, and we develop a universal framework with relative deviations $O(m^{-1/4}\ln^{\varepsilon}m)$ and $O(m^{-1/2}\ln^{\varepsilon}m)$ to address the general and non-negative matrix cases respectively. The given framework addresses the specified problem as well as two related but more complex issues, and we introduce two efficient algorithms based on the framework for computing the type-approximating matrix. The presented bounds are distinct and comprehensive since they are unconditional and the best possible, and we verify the optimality of the general matrix type-approximation result by reaching the one-order lower bound limit. Furthermore, we obtain a generalized type-conversion matrix bound for any intermediate matrix type, and we address a number and type challenge that involves a deviation estimation in a graph for its closest distance to a graph that can be represented using $d$ specific nodes. We found an optimal bound for the d = 2 case but presented a logarithmically inferior bound for the d > 2 case. We developed a new algorithm for graph approximation which reaches the non-universal type-conversion matrix bound for all d >= 2, and we showed the impossibility of achieving the universal bound by reaching a certain lower bound limit. The computed bound is 2 to the power of the number of nodes in the graph, which is a logarithmically inferior than the universal bound. We developed a new lossless transformation from the universal 4-approximation algorithm for the max-cut and min-half-cycle problems into 2-approximating algorithms for the distance to d-cuts and half-cycles, and we showed the possibility of computing these problems in polynomial time when d is equal to two but reached a pseudo-polynomial time when d is greater than two. We found lower and upper bounds for the constructibility of protocols with a small transmission rate for the bounded-valued quantized protocol, and we obtained a description for the achievable transmission rate when it is possible to compute such protocols. We found that there exists a protocol which allows us to compute the type and number challenge in $O(m^{3/2}\ln^3m)$

A novel approach for creating these emitters involves using ESR mapping to precisely locate the positions of spin-sensitive defect clusters in silicon. By positioning these defects at the optimal distance from the silicon-radiation interface, the recombination efficiency of quantum emitters can be maximized. A specific protocol for achieving this optimal distance involves implanting fluorine atoms prior to the formation of silicon nanowires. By analyzing the distribution of these implanted fluorine atoms via the NMRX technique, the positions of the spin-sensitive defect clusters can be predicted. A case in point involves the successful implementation of this protocol at the Mark II fabrication facility. There, the precision with which the distribution of implanted fluorine atoms was replicated in silicon nanowires directly influenced the distance between the centers of quantum emitters and the silicon-radiation interface. This problem is even more complicated when the tasks are unrelated and there's a significant drift in the data from one task to another. Despite existing research, a suitable memory-efficient and computationally lightweight solution is still a topic of debate. In our study, we evaluated and compared several such methods: i) revisiting past tasks infrequently, ii) using a fixed memory limit, iii) relying on a fixed processing time, and iv) using a self-adaptive approach to balance processing time and memory usage. Our goal was to identify which strategy would be most effective, as well as how the system's performance was influenced by different stream lengths, memory constraints, and processing time thresholds. Using synthetic data, we conducted a thorough analysis and provided novel insights into the performance trade-offs of these memory-efficient and computationally lightweight methods. The findings indicated that a systematic approach to continuing learning on a stream of tasks exists, but it's highly dependent on several factors including the specific datasets used, memory constraints, and processing time limits. Ultimately, we identified areas for further improvement and proposed challenges and future research directions in this area.  As part of our study, we developed and shared an open-source Python-based simulator to support our investigation into the suitability of these memory-efficient and computationally lightweight continual learning methods. The code is hosted under the terms of the MIT License and is available at:  https://github.com/jhernandezp/continual-learning-simulator.git.  This simulator provides a flexible means of exploring, comparing, and evaluating the performance of various memory-efficient and computationally lightweight continual learning methods, as well as helping researchers to design new techniques aimed at improving the efficiency of continuing learning on a stream of tasks. We will demonstrate that the completeness theorem for first-order logic also leads to Gödel's first incompleteness theorem as a consequence. To achieve this goal, we must demonstrate that the completeness theorem for first-order logic implies the compactness theorem for first-order logic. The compactness theorem, in turn, enables the construction of a theory that includes a sentence in arithmetic with undecidable model. This achievement is a result of a thorough examination and proof of a long-standing debate posited by Solovay. We will show that the reverse relationship between these three theorems - completeness, compactness, and incompleteness - is also reciprocal. Specifically, we will prove that the compactness theorem implies the completeness theorem for first-order logic with respect to countable languages, but the reverse is not valid. Similarly, we will demonstrate that Gödel's first incompleteness theorem implies the compactness theorem, but the reverse is also not true. Consequently, we will utilize Gödel's first incompleteness theorem as an alternative means to demonstrate the compactness theorem and derive the completeness theorem for first-order logic. Ultimately, this sequence of relationships will allow us to address and resolve a number of fundamental questions in the well-known Posner's debate on the comparative powers of first-order logic and arithmetic that has been ongoing for decades. In contrast to Posner's work, our derivation is language-independent. We will demonstrate that first-order logic is, in fact, stronger than arithmetic with respect to certain model-theoretic features, but we will also show that the difference in model-theoretic features is not the only factor contributing to the differential expressive power of first-order logic and arithmetic. We will achieve this distinction by identifying the underlying logical relationships between the distinct types of models and their respective logics that give rise to differential expressive power. In doing so, we will broaden our understanding of the interaction between model theory, logic, and philosophy. hidden variables. It's a decision-making scenario where observers have incomplete
information about both the underlying system states and the random factors
driving the market. At each stage, these observers learn about the current system
states through relative new information, and their investment decisions are
influenced by both their understanding of the market dynamics and their belief in
the hidden variables. To facilitate decision-making, a learning-based approach
is employed to update beliefs and a deep Q-network is trained to develop a
policy. My results show the effectiveness of this approach in addressing multi-stage
portfolio selection with hidden variables. Additionally, I examine cases with
known market dynamics and incomplete observations to establish relationships
between key metrics, such as dynamic programming's optimality condition and
conditional entropy. These connections illuminate the impact of partial
observations on portfolio selection when market dynamics are well understood.
Furthermore, I explore two applications of these findings. Firstly, I establish a
method for reconstructing the true system states using only relative new
information, and secondly, I develop a model that predicts investment returns
based on partial observations of the true system states using a convolutional neural
network. These applications demonstrate that learning to choose the best portfolio
under incomplete observations of the hidden variables can also provide insights
about the system dynamics and its states. The research is further advanced by
introducing 'context information', which is a measurement that closely relates to
the hidden variables and is accessible to learn. By incorporating context information
into the Q-network's learning, it is shown that context information can either
enhance or reduce the benefit it provides to portfolio selection depending on the
specific nature of the context. Thus, it is identified as a double-edged sword in
portfolio selection with hidden variables. Lastly, I establish a connection between
conditional diffusion models and portfolio selection. By utilizing the diffusion
process to sample true system states from an anormali distribution, it is shown
that choosing a portfolio based on incomplete observations can still provide
optimal results if the context information regarding the hidden variables is also
provided. The finding is further verified on real data. The code used for this

This study examined the relationship between measured cognitive complexity and the overall number of lines in programs across various algorithms to determine if there's a link. Three programming languages were chosen: Java, Python, and C, for which popular lexic graphs were analyzed with respect to a benchmark of 249 algorithms. Surprisingly, the results showed that cognitive complexity peaked and then plateaued at moderate program sizes, suggesting that complex programs are not necessarily larger. This implies that other factors contribute to cognitive complexity, such as algorithmic issues. Interestingly, the results also indicated that algorithms with higher cognitive complexity tend to have lower test coverage ratios, suggesting a link between these factors. Furthermore, the study investigated the impact of language-specific features, including type systems, that could influence cognitive complexity. While size-independent factors were sought after, the results showed that the simplest language, Python, which lacks explicit type definitions, did not exhibit the observed plateau effect, nor did it have the best test coverage ratio. Overall, the study highlights the importance of algorithmic considerations in understanding cognitive complexity and encourages researchers to explore ways to mitigate its negative effects on program understanding, even at moderate program sizes. As a secondary contribution, the study's results provide a foundation for answering complex questions in interactive code reading tasks and suggest that cognitive complexity could be a valuable metric for evaluating these tasks. Finally, the study's analysis of popular static analysis tools showed that they effectively identify complex parts of programs but fail to forecast cognitive complexity, a metric that is still poorly understood. As a result, the study proposes a novel static analysis framework, named Alceo, that dynamically explores the neighbourhood of each procedure to assess cognitive complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that Alceo delivers accurate predictions of cognitive complexity with moderate computational overhead. By combining Alceo's predictions with other static analysis tools, the study achieved an average of 94% accuracy in classifying 75% of the benchmark algorithms as easy or hard to understand. As a result, the study recommends employing Alceo's predictions as a supplementary tool to guide, for instance, the complexity-reducing refactoring of programs. The study's code, data, and Alceo's framework have been made available on the GitHub platform. As a joint theoretical and experimental study, the findings provide an invaluable framework for evaluating and guiding the complexity of software systems, a topic that is still under active research in the field of Software

Nonetheless, there are still concerns that these metrics can be unfair as they may penalize certain types of linguistic variations that are not reflected in the reference standard, raising issues about how to strike a balance between translating accurately and adhering to reference guidelines.  To address these concerns, we developed a novel metric that evaluates a whole corpus of translations fairly by considering each sentence within the context of the surrounding sentences.  Specifically, our method employs a context-based attention mechanism inspired by how humans understand written text and uses reference sentences to set a corporate standard for translation quality, thereby providing a fair evaluation of the entire corpus even when linguistic variations occur.  To test the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a study comparing it to other state-of-the-art metrics on various datasets and also conducted a new survey to gather more human judgments to supplement existing evaluation datasets.  The results show that our method is as effective as other top-performing metrics in terms of accuracy and also provides a more fair evaluation of different referencing standards.  Moreover, our method outperforms other metrics when it comes to evaluating the quality of different human annotations, demonstrating its value in tapping into human judgment to assess various aspects of translation quality.  Ultimately, our method is compatible with existing instruction-based machine translation and can be used in conjunction with other evaluation methods to provide a more comprehensive view of different referencing standards and human annotation datasets. Our analysis utilizes both 1D spectral simulations and 2D hydrodynamic simulations to examine the electromagnetic emission from these relativistic shocks. In a continuous electron-positron system, our 1D spectral models reveal a distinct splitting of synchrotron X-ray bands, separated by a gap, which is a consequence of differing electron and positron spectra. However, this unique band structure is compromised by particle diffusion and fragmentation resulting from shock cycle oscillations in systems with uneven gas distribution. Utilizing 2D hydrodynamic simulations, our research reveals the complex behavior of relativistic shock cycles. Despite these cycles exhibiting periodic oscillations with irregular periods, our radio/X-ray light curve analysis indicates that the emission patterns lack a distinct periodic structure. Instead, shock strength, rather than cycle frequency, is the dominant factor influencing light curves. Our research also includes a comprehensive comparison with the gamma ray burst afterglow model. Furthermore, our analysis addresses the potential detection of polarization in synchrotron emission from these radiative shock waves driven by relativistic pairs. Due to uniform and symmetric matter distribution in these systems, our anticipation is that the polarization axis would be oriented along the forward direction, however, this expectation may be compromised by diffuse and fragmented matter which could result in variable and unpredictable polarization axis orientations. Ultimately showing that radiative shock waves driven in a continuous relativistic pair plasma offer an appealing, yet unconventional alternative to afterglow models. $^{40}$Ca atoms in various hyperfine states with specific spin configurations, placed in an optical lattice with two sites. Our study examines how to utilize this system and a accompanying gauge field resulting from spin-orbit coupling to implement a theoretical model of a Dirac oscillator. We specifically investigate how interactions between light and matter, resulting in spontaneous emission, affect this model. To achieve this, we incident a resonant laser beam into the system to trigger a phenomenon where the gauge field simulating a heavy particle influences the lighter particles' behavior in accordance with a heavy Dirac oscillator model. Due to the lighter mass in the second site, we observe a spatial separation of the two-component wave function. Upon analysis of the gauge field's influence, we find that its presence does not significantly impact the mixture's level repulsion. Our research shows that an ultra-cold cold atoms system can effectively mimic a heavy Dirac oscillator behavior.  We also propose using the heavy Dirac oscillator to develop a precise measurement technique for angular momentum within optical traps. By radiating a monochromatic light into the system, we can observe a transition from a Dirac oscillator-like behavior to a mixture of coherent states. Furthermore, our research suggests that this transition can be manipulated via the Rabi oscillation to achieve coherent superpositions of angular momentum within optical traps.  By further refining this coherent superposition, we can perfectly measure the angular momentum within optical traps. Using the models of a heavy Dirac oscillator and an angular momentum coherences measure, we propose a new method for measuring angular momentum by shooting a directed beam into the mixture, which has also been verified by an numerical simulation.  A direct beam will cause a superconductivity transition, and the time evolution of the superconductivity will be controlled by the gauge field.  By controlling the directed beam and the gauge field, we can measure the angular momentum.  The major advantage of this method over traditional methods for measuring angular momentum within optical traps is that it does not require complicated equipment or a large amount of money.  Rather, this method requires a simple setup and relatively low costs as compared to other methods.  Lastly, we also propose another method for measuring angular momentum by using a heavy Dirac oscillator to drive a quantum teleportation process, which has also been verified by an numerical simulation.  By controlling the gauge field and a directed beam, we can measure the quantum state at a remote location which will be further verified by analyzing the two-component wave function and the population of the two hyperfine states.

However, the necessary negative energy density cannot be achieved with our current technological capabilities. Despite this, the drive's mathematical constraints have significant implications for achieving it. Prior research has suggested that quantum effects alone may be insufficient to generate the required spacetime, but could potentially enable timely access to a region where the drive is feasible. Our research investigates whether quantum gravity and gravity manipulation capabilities are necessary to implement the Alcubierre drive. By analyzing the drive's constraints within a simplified framework, we demonstrate that the required spacetime can be achieved with a moderate level of timeliness, which can be quantified using a scalar variable. If the variable remains positive, the spacetime is viable; if negative, the spacetime is unattainable. However, the variable's magnitude is heavily dependent on the initial spacetime's parameters. With precise data or fine-tuning the initial parameters, the spacetime becomes attainable. Conversely, the variable's sign is determined by local energy conditions, which are violated in the center of the drive. Despite this, the variable can be improved, allowing the spacetime to become viable. However, the variable's ultimate limit is set by an integral of the curvature's magnitude, which is inevitably reached as the spacetime evolves. A novel approach for modifying the variable's value involves introducing a scalar wormhole into the Alcubierre spacetime, which can be achieved by imposing a condition on the variable's value. Interestingly, the required scalar wormhole's shape and geometry can be designed using the variable's parameters, which highlights the significant impact of initial spacetime parameters. Furthermore, introducing a scalar wormhole yields a spacetime that is inevitably closed, whereas various configurations are possible. Additionally, the existing Alcubierrie drive already incorporates aspects of a scalar wormhole, which arises from rearranging the variable's equation.   The process of creating these proposals, which are referred to as Motions, is typically governed by specific rules in most online communities where they are employed.
  These rules specifically influence how long a fully formed motion remains visible to new users.
  This study aims to examine the effect of reformulating workshop policies on the uptake of MOT motions, which are essentially proposals for discourse changes, in an experiment. 
  To achieve this, an experiment was conducted on the Discourse platform, a popular software for online community management, by introducing an experiment group where the default timing of the MOT vote was altered from 7 days to 30 days and comparing it to a control group with the original 7-day timing. 
  The outcome of the experiment showed that extending the vote duration led to a 1.6% increase in the number of MOTs proposed, a 42% increase in the number of votes received, and a 3.2% increase in the percentage of voted-up MOTs that were eventually adopted. 
  The corresponding decrease in the number of MOTs that were inactive during their vote also supported the efficacy of the prolonged vote duration. 
  The results suggest that providing a more extended period for voting can be a valuable strategy for boosting the effectiveness of motivated users who seek to implement positive discourse changes. 
  The corresponding decrease in the number of MOTs that were inactive during their vote also verified that users require sufficient time to engage with and react to proposals for discourse changes. 
  The observed validation of the adopted MOTs also validated the feasibility of extending the vote duration for motivating users. 
  The most notable advantage of the prolonged vote duration is that it allows more time for users to discover and react to proposals for discourse changes, which are typically formulated in response to community-specific circumstances. 
  The results of the experiment are, therefore, consistent with the typical nature of the evolution of Discourse platforms, which exhibit periodic periods of increased activity driven by community members who initiate discourse changes through MOTs. 
  The corresponding empirical observations of the Discourse community also validated the anticipation that an extended vote duration would result in a higher number of votes for active MOTs, which are viewed as integral to the evolution of the community. 
  The discovered positive outcomes of the prolonged vote duration are, therefore, consistent with the typical motivations and behaviors of users who are active in initiating discourse changes through MOTs, which is to enhance their community.

The bounded variable section is an especially challenging subset with extensive use in fields such as optimization, statistical analysis, and coding theory.  Currently, the standard tool for handling these systems is the sparse elimination method, which involves eliminating variables based on the degree of their associated polynomials.  However, this approach is not optimized for solving the bounded variable section, as it lacks the capability to eliminate variables beyond its current bound.  In order to address this limitation, we have developed an enhanced approach, SEBVS, which integrates the sparse elimination method with an additional linear algebra component, thereby expanding the range of variables that can be eliminated.  By eliminating more variables, SEBVS also has the added benefit of eliminating variable sets that exceed the original bound.  In addition to SEBVS, we have also introduced a second strategy, Local SEBVS, which integrates a local search function to enhance the performance of SEBVS in eliminating variables.  By eliminating additional variables, SEBVS and Local SEBVS have shown superior results in comparison to the existing approaches for solving bounded variable section, with the experiments and results demonstrating their efficient processing of large datasets in addition to providing detailed analytical insights into their performance. A noise channel is a mathematical concept that maps genuine data to one or
more incorrect values, representing errors that occur during data collection.
Many noise channels involve noise that destroys original data, resulting in new
values that don't reflect the underlying data distribution.  A well-known example
is label flipping, which is a noise channel that exchanges class labels.  Although
not typically viewed as a noise channel, this type of noise can be considered
one.  We investigate whether destruction noise channels can be mitigated and, if
possible, how to implement such a mitigation strategy.  A successful method would
preserve the original data distribution in the noise effects.  We demonstrate the
feasibility of mitigating destruction noise channels using a simple, efficient
technique called "destruction learning".  This method combines the corrupted labels
with unsupervised learning to generate a noise-corrected class label distribution.
We prove that our mitigation strategy is effective and efficient in destruction noise
channels that destroy class labels and are manageable on average.  A new, simple
algorithm is introduced, demonstrating its practical utility in overcoming the constraints
of degradation noise channels that destroy original data values.  A well-known algorithm,

best techniques available and that it is comparable to training a robust model in the

the data distribution is unknown or inaccessible.  We also apply our technique to
four applications, including two that were previously unrelated to destruction noise
channels, such as detecting deepfakes and reducing nearest neighbor query costs.

developing a successful mitigation method for other destruction noise channels, such

common English idiom referring to two objects that share a single quality. It's used to indicate that one object is essentially another. This phrase is similar to "birds of a feather," which also connotes the idea of two things being essentially the same. Another comparable idiom is "the pot calling the kettle black," implying that both objects are equally guilty of the same offense. In contrast to these phrases, "you are what you eat" suggests that one object can transform into another, whereas "an apple for the teacher" is more of a metaphor that equates two things with one another using exchange value. Lastly, "all's well that ends well" is more of a proverb that doesn't directly compare two things, but rather provides a moral or a piece of advice. Ultimately, these idioms are unique in their own characteristics, but they all serve to add flavor and depth to the English language without providing a literal meaning. They are utilized to convey complex and context-dependent meanings, and they can be effectively employed in various situations. A crucial aspect to consider when using these idiomatic expressions is the non-monotonic nature of their interpretation, which means that changing one semantic component may cause the interpretation to change as well. For example, replacing "night and day" with "light and heat" would result in a new interpretation. To determine the correct interpretation of an idiom, both its literal and metaphorical meanings must be taken into account. If the metaphorical meaning of the idiom is that two things are essentially the same, then the new variation "light and heat" may very well be a valid use of the idiom, whereas "place and time" clearly is not. The "benchmark" is actually an obfuscation, as "Meta-Benchmarking" would be a more accurate term. Unlike conventional evaluation on distinct datasets, this benchmark conducts the same analysis on the same dataset, testing views on the same data without true progress. In the context of NLP, conventional evaluation involves analyzing a dataset and presenting results, as is typical with LAMBADA and SuperGLUE. To prevent misleading conclusions about the efficacy of a view, we have developed Meta-Benchmarking, designed to be applied until a truly distinct dataset is identified. Until that time, Meta-Benchmarking is a necessary step in advancing NLP research. We have introduced a new benchmark that defies easy categorization into traditional NLP problems, as it is a form of Meta-Benchmarking. We have presented an innovative pipeline-based approach called pipe-view, specifically tailored for in-memory graph analysis, and tested it within the Meta-Benchmarking framework on a selected dataset. The outcome of this exercise has exposed shortcomings in current NLP tools, as well as opportunities for positive change. The Meta-Benchmarking challenge can be viewed as a call to action, inviting the NLP research community to address three areas: improving our selection of dataset benchmarks, enhancing the transparency of research results, and filling the gap in available analysis tools that are suitable for in-memory graph analysis. The dataset and corresponding view source code are available at https://github.com/PipeView/Plot49. A temporary web-based platform has been established at https://www.plot49.com to serve as a testing ground for Meta-Benchmarking, allowing viewers to conduct their own analyses and participate in the ongoing study. The plot at the heart of Meta-Benchmarking is quite simple: graph data that represents researcher collaborations has been collecting dust in our local repositories for years, and we have only now developed a computational pipeline to analyze this data. As a result, we have uncovered a number of interesting patterns, such as a statistically significant correlation between a researcher's popularity and their propensity to respond to comments, as well as a notable disparity between a researcher's paper counts and citation counts. The Meta-Benchmarking platform will be used to conduct an ongoing study that involves the following components: 1) analyzing new data, such as book purchases that involve in-memory graph analysis, 2) inviting a select group of researchers to analyze the data, 3) monitoring the outcomes of their analyses, and 4) updating the platform with new features based on the insights gained

traffic flow estimation through video analysis has gained prominence in vehicle routing and parking space detection applications. Traditional p-frame detection methods mainly rely on deep learning techniques like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), which demand substantial labeled data for training. Moreover, they tend to be susceptible to class imbalance. This paper introduces an application-driven p-frame detection method that incorporates spatial temporal attention for identifying inactive vehicles. It proposes an end-to-end network consisting of two branches - a CNN-based feature extraction module shared with a one-shot detector, and a scalable matching module with spatial temporal attention. This enables the network to select high-quality negative samples and eliminate noisy samples, thereby enhancing scalability and accuracy. Above all, the end-to-end network offers a real-time p-frame detection performance at 94.04% and 70.85% in terms of F1-score and average precision at 95th percentile, respectively. It also boasts high detection speed of 53.41 frames per second. Human experts have reviewed the application-related p-frame data and provided feedback. Based on their feedback, we have further optimized the proposed method and achieved better results compared to state-of-the-art methods. More specifically, the tail performance has been improved to 94.00% and 71.29% in terms of F1-score and average precision at 95th percentile, respectively. The proposed method has also been applied in two real-world vehicle routing scenarios and yielded satisfactory outcomes. It is expected that the method may experience degradation on roads with extremely low speed limits. To further improve the method, it is suggested to use ground truth speed limits instead of the average speed of inactive vehicles. Furthermore, it is hoped that in the future, ground truth speed limits can be automatically obtained. We resolve a significant technical hurdle posed by the stochastic domain's one-dimensional geometry and establish strong convergence of the stochastic equation's solutions under local and uniform Lipschitz conditions. Our findings allow the stochastic equation to converge to its deterministic analogue, ensuring the stochastic equation's solutions exhibit unique, pathwise stability. The introduced framework supports the transfer of surface information along with Gaussian process-based shape and pose data. Evaluations on the BMS 36 dataset and the 4D human dataset reveal that using the proposed framework results in greater accuracy than employing traditional surface registration techniques within our dataset. Audio vector networks (AVNs) have shown great potential in source localization by embedding spatial information in the feature space of the input signals. However, estimating 3D angles from wide-array recordings is a challenging task due to the inherent ambiguities inherent in directional microphones. This paper presents a model that leverages audio vector networks while addressing the inherent ambiguities of directional microarrays. A novel loss function is proposed that can handle these ambiguities and is tested on scenes20v2 dataset. Compared to existing loss functions, this approach achieves higher average spatial accuracy of 2.25 degrees for azimuth and 3.07 degrees for elevation. Additionally, a model using this loss function outperforms a baseline model by 0.23 in spatial reciprocal signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). It is observed that existing loss functions, although simple, already achieve substantial source localization performance and further improvements yield only marginal enhancements of 0.4 to 0.6 degrees in spatial error. Importantly, the proposed loss function outperforms existing methods without requiring large-scale datasets like gorham-audio for model training. As a result, this approach has the potential to simplify the process of source localization research. A repository containing the code is available at the link: https://github.com/gsghoram/avlambdas. Follow-up research is being planned to further improve the performance of audio vector networks in source localization by addressing the challenge of directional ambiguities and by leveraging vectorization of complex numbers for processing complex data. various types of displacement and transformation, such as translations, rotations, scaling, and other types like bending and stretching. Registering these various warps poses a significant challenge. One way to approach this problem is by simplifying the problem into separate components - translation, rotation, scaling, and other type of displacement. Studies have shown that translating, rotating, and scaling are the most common types of displacement in data such as speech, cardiovascular signals, and genomic data. To register only these three types of displacement, we can utilize two approaches: 1) a frequency approach where we translate, rotate, and scale in frequency domain, 2) a parameterized approach where we model translation, rotate, and scale using real-valued functions. Both approaches have been used to register functional data such as resting-state brain function networks. However, the frequency approach has been used in registering periodic data such as periodical physiological signals. Registering data with non-periodic pattern requires an advanced approach which involves using a non-linear optimization algorithm like the DALC algorithm to register data such as daily activity patterns. Studies show that we can increase the model's ability to identify accurate registrations by using the model to calculate a gradient map that indicates where the displacement occurs. This process, when combined with the model's robustness, can increase the model's scalability by reducing the number of functional data when sampled sparsely. Registering data with scaling requires the use of a different approach, the R-DALC algorithm, which is based on a non-linear orthogonal transformation. Studies show that using orthogonal transformation increases the model's ability to identify accurate registrations. Furthermore, the non-linear non-linear R-DALC algorithm, when combined with the model's robustness, increases the model's scalability by reducing the number of functional data when sampled sparsely. Registering data with non-periodic patterns using non-linear non-linear R-DALC yields a superior performance to previous algorithms. For instance, in a simulation study, registered daily activity patterns using non-linear non-linear R-DALC yield a superior.026 average correlation between original and registered data compared to.034,.044, and.051 for Deep-LLC, Low-LLC, and High-LLC respectively. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in R packages dalc and rdalc. The corresponding code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jorgehcifuentes/dalc, https://github.com/jorgehcifuentes/rdalc. A major obstacle is the time-consuming process of locating potential datasets, often requiring multiple years of preparation and research planning. A valuable solution lies in data discovery portals that streamline the process of identifying and selecting datasets suitable for research objectives. Nevertheless, these portals face difficulties in efficiently processing and indexing large datasets, resulting in unacceptably prolonged query times for users. In response, researchers have proposed various data discovery systems with distinct architecture choices. This article aims to provide researchers with an in-depth overview of current data discovery systems, evaluating their merits and drawbacks through the lens of (1) data representation and (2) query processing algorithms. By examining a multitude of papers spanning more than a decade, this survey seeks to offer insights on how existing systems can be improved to enhance the discovery of scientific data and accelerate the innovation process. As such, this article may serve as a starting point for future advancements in this area, with the ultimate goal of expanding the repertoire of existing systems to foster more effective discovery tools and accelerate scientific advancements. The survey is accompanied by an open-source repository containing the source of all figures as well as compiled versions of the papers examined during this research initiative. It is readily accessible via the GitHub platform at: https://github.com/jorge-ramos/data-discovery-survey. Furthermore, by providing the compiled code in conjunction with the platform, it is hoped that the research community can engage with this research through issues, pull requests and discussions. The metapopulation SEIR model addresses this need, incorporating detailed information about geographic areas, population density, gathering locations, and other vital data, which enables the tracking of transmission dynamics at the regional level, ultimately guiding resource allocation to contain the pandemic.  Although the basic SEIR model is applied worldwide, traditional formulations neglect the intricate dynamics between regions, and more importantly, they fail to account for the critical role of community spread, which often results in an underestimation of virus incidence and mortality predictions.  In contrast, our refined metapulsecular SEIR model addresses these limitations by introducing external virus introductions and intra-regional self-sustained transmission dynamics, incorporating data on migration within the regional network.  This model was applied to the Italian pandemic outbreak, and under our updated transmission dynamics, our simulations exhibit a striking correlation with the actual data, as evidenced by the fit of virus curves at the national and regional levels.  The close match between predicted and actual data is attributed to the simultaneous introduction of contagion risks through movement within and between regions, and our simulation demonstrates that this spread may have begun as early as February-March 2020, well before the official surge in cases.  The success of our model in capturing the essence of virus transmission dynamics through regional network simulations will aid in the analysis of other pandemic outbreaks, providing a foundation for modeling epidemiological data.  Furthermore, our simulation highlights the significant role of community spread, emphasizing the need for timely isolation of close contacts to contain the pandemic, as evidenced by the substantial decrease in predicted cases following the lockdown on March 21, 2020.  Finally, our simulation exhibits a robust resilience in predicted virus curves that outperforms other models not accounting for regional connectivity and community spread.  The remarkable success of our model in predicting virus transmission dynamics and case evolution necessitates the revision of current incidence and mortality predictions, necessitating a rapid surge in medical responses. Additionally, CSI provides a comprehensive representation of environmental distortions and noise, complementing the geometric structure learned by DNNs. Existing CSI-based localization methods have employed deep learning alone, missed opportunities to integrate learning from CSI data due to its channel matrix form.  To capitalize on this potential, we introduce a distance metric focused on channel angle shifts that is naturally interpretable and informative about environmental distortions and noise.  Furthermore, we develop an enhanced localization method called SAMN-DBN, combining a dimensionality-reduced multiplicative attention network with a dynamic bimodal hidden Markov model.  This model has the ability to model complex temporal transitions while identifying signal occurrences and periods of silence, thereby robustly localizing in dynamic and noisy scenarios.  Our evaluation reveals that the proposed method surpasses current benchmarks in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.  Code and model implementations are available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/lienewbie/DBHMM/tree/database-dependent.  To address data scarcity, we also introduce a method for generating training data based on channel path loss models, demonstrating that this approach is both time and memory efficient.  Finally, our analysis of the performance of the base learner demonstrates that integrating CSI with deep learning leads to significantly improved localization accuracy.  Lastly, we found that the dynamic behavior of the deep and attention models to be slighter greater than the deep model alone.  However, we believe that the slight increased complexity is a worthwhile trade-off for the enhanced robustness, increased interpretability and increased theoretical understandability of the models.  We hope that our method will inspire researchers to integrate learning from CSI into channel-based localization research.  We look forward to seeing the practical applications of our method in real-world scenarios.  We intend to share our datasets and code for this work at https://github.com/lienewbie/DBHMM. However, when dealing with large-scale graphs that exceed memory capacity, incorporating the full neighbor information becomes impractical due to a high memory footprint. A common strategy for processing such graphs involves sampling neighbors using techniques such as sampling based on degrees, random sampling, and structural sampling. These methods can effectively reduce the memory footprint, albeit often resulting in a loss in generalization accuracy. This work aims to address this accuracy trade-off by presenting a novel method for improving the mean relative precision (MRP) for GNN samplers. By analyzing the sampling process as a noise factor affecting model outputs, we have developed a technique for estimating sampler-induced noise. Based on this estimate, we have created a loss function that measures sampler noise and can be used to train samplers with improved performance. Furthermore, we have devised an approach for distributing this trained sampler noise among classes, creating a noise-aware GNN classifier. Our experimental results have confirmed the efficacy of our method, demonstrating improved accuracy when combined with existing sampling methods in the context of node classification tasks. As a complementary tool, the code for implementing our method can be found on the repository at https://github.com/jie Shen22/learnable-sampler. This code enables researchers to reproduce our paper's experiments and assess the practical implications of our method.
