the root analysis utility framework, known as rootpy, is a Python package designed to simplify analysis tasks based on the root data storage format, which is used by the CERN's Particle Physics Research Council. rootpy facilitates data processing by providing a programming interface that is consistent with standard Python data handling practices. It enhances data visualization, enables file management with descriptive metadata, and streamlines data analysis with NumPy and SciPy integration. rootpy and its accompanying plotter class are compatible with Asymptotic Monte Carlo simulations and include functionality for generating Monte Carlo truth files. This version includes several analysis utility enhancements, visualization improvements, and added functionality for generating Monte Carlo truth files. rootpy version 1.6.0 is available through the PyPI package manager for easy installation, and includes full documentation including user guides, API reference, and a sample analysis demonstration. 

  We have introduced the plotter class, which is rootpy's central data visualization tool, to efficiently create static and dynamic plots for common analysis tasks. rootpy includes a range of pre-defined plot templates that can be quickly applied to custom plots, and provides a customizable plotting interface that is compatible with the plotter class. 

  rootpy and its related packages, rootpy_plotter and rootpy_analysis, contribute to the SciPy and NumPy libraries by integrating established analysis tools and utilities into the distribution package framework. rootpy includes a collection of root data analysis utilities that provide efficient computing performance, and exposes underlying CERN root API functions through the pyroot package for manual access. 

  We have integrated the Monte Carlo integration package, imbinet, into the rootpy distribution, which provides efficient Bayesian network inference for general and particle physics-specific problems. Additionally, we have incorporated the rat package, which is used for rating the relevance of event descriptions in statistical calculations. 

  rootpy includes a number of sub-packages that provide essential tools for root data analysis, including path utilities, file metadata services, and root data converters for efficient computing. The package has been used in the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC to analyze particle physics data. As a result, this analysis utility package receives regular updates that incorporate industry-standard best practices, as well as contributions from a diverse group of users. 

  rootpy and its associated packages, available through PyPI, are easily installed using the standard package manager. We have included the rootpy documentation, including user guides, API reference, and a demonstration analysis in the package distribution, which is available through the link provided in the documentation

Our study focuses on the content moderation of online discussion platforms, particularly Reddit, which combines both topic-specific'subreddits' and global networks of communities, known as comments and submissions. We examine the composition of communities that moderate content, evaluating the effectiveness of their actions, and whether such roles can influence member behavior. We analyze how community involvement in content moderation impacts user engagement, using a within-variance design to assess the effects of moderation involvement on user behavior across subreddite and r2 communities. We discovered that users in communities that engage in content moderation, as measured by moderator status, comment frequency, and engagement in moderation-related activities, tend to have higher levels of involvement. We also investigated whether moderation policies influence member behavior, through both content-based and behavioral analysis of six key subreddite, focusing on strict, open, and neutral communities. Our findings suggest that, although users in content-moderating communities may be more prone to engage negatively, the effect of community involvement on content is actually more significant than the risk of negativity, and nearly twice as great as the influence of user personality traits. We revealed a crucial distinction between content-moderating and non-content-moderating subreddite, with the latter often allowing toxic comments to persist. We analyzed the interaction between Reddit's automated comment filtering system and human moderators in four subreddite, demonstrating that content-moderating communities are more likely to successfully employ the comments' filtering system to eliminate negativity. Our study provides essential insights for designing and maintaining large-scale online conversational spaces. Finally, our results imply that providing users with clear guidelines for online discourse, supplemented with automated tools, can be effective in promoting cohesion and negative-free interaction. Our study highlights the importance of reconsidering the traditional 1-1-1 model for online conversations, with one community governing discourse, one set of rules, and one central topic of interest. We propose the 2-2-infinity model as an alternative, featuring two distinct communities with overlapping interests, two sets of community-specific guidelines, and an open-ended set of rules that evolve dynamically. The first community is involved in content moderation, ensuring the discussion remains on-track and free from negativity. The second community focuses on maintaining the conversation, shaping its direction, and refining its rules through iterative feedback and collaboration.

This study examines the transfer of biased knowledge from pre-trained language models to downstream tasks. We contend that models incorporating biased knowledge in pre-training will also exhibit biased knowledge transfer to downstream tasks. We have made our data and code available for further research.  We conducted extensive experiments to reduce over-fitting and obtained results from these experiments.  We developed a method to decrease biased knowledge transfer but our proposed technique failed to yield significant results.  We found that models commonly used as weak supervision in real-world applications tend to exhibit biased knowledge transfer.  We discovered that models possessing less complexity, such as sparsely activated models, also possess biased knowledge transfer.  We explored the influence of dataset size on biased knowledge transfer and observed a decrease in biased knowledge transfer with a larger dataset.  We identified models with contradictory knowledge as a potential means to eradicate biased knowledge transfer. We developed an interactive system allowing users to select an adapter that removes biased knowledge transfer from pre-trained models and downstream tasks. We developed an automatic adapter that removes biased knowledge transfer based on the diversity of outputs in downstream tasks and applied it to multiple datasets. In many instances, evaluating the probability $p(x)$ is particularly challenging or even unfeasible. This research investigates Bayesian estimation in scenarios where only aggregate loss functions, which are comprised of conditional density functions, can be utilized to derive probabilistic insights. As these functions are incapable of capturing uncertainty, they are viewed as ineffective tools in Bayesian inference. Contrary to this perception, it is demonstrated that Bayesian methods can still provide meaningful parameter estimates and intervals characterized by uncertainty ranges. To achieve this, aggregate loss functions are utilized to optimize objectives incorporating both precision and recall metrics, thereby facilitating informed hypothesis testing using these estimates. Experimental findings are presented to substantiate the efficacy of the proposed approach. Furthermore, the subject is further broadened by formulating the issue as a multi-objective optimization problem where multiple estimators are identified to optimize different objectives simultaneously. This is particularly relevant in situations where bias and variance trade-offs are inherent in aggregate loss functions. By identifying Pareto-efficient Bayesian estimators, it is shown that: (i) unbiased estimators are included in the optimal set, and (ii) the proposed approach is capable of tackling common Bayesian estimation challenges. This transformation utilizes a specific photonic device with integrated two-phase modulators, enabling the accurate recreation of arbitrary two-photon amplitudes in an orthonormal "J-matrix" basis through Fourier inversion. In this system, orthonormal photon number states serve as the "J-matrix" basis, and the corresponding "J-matrix" itself contains the coupling coefficients of a Jacobi polynomial that mirrors the process of quantum teleportation via a two-photon cat state channel. This system is utilized to achieve high-fidelity measurements of two quantum states originating from a continuous input source. Furthermore, the concept of the J-matrix system offers a viable method for addressing the challenges posed by multi-photon nonlinearity in photonic quantum computing and communication. 

  We experimentally demonstrate the successful transformation of a two-photon state into a two-quantum-bit qudit state. This is achieved using a photonic J-matrix system which utilizes a photonic device with integrated two-phase modulators to accurately recreate the two-photon state amplitudes in an orthonormal "J-matrix" basis. 

  We present the theoretical characteristics of a photonic J-matrix system that consists of a collection of orthonormal photon number states and their corresponding "J-matrix" coupling coefficients, mirroring the process of quantum teleportation via a two-photon cat state channel. 

  We numerically investigate the capabilities of the photonic J-matrix system in measuring the effects of two-photon nonlinearity in a photonic quantum computing circuit, demonstrating its ability to efficiently decode complex, multi-qubit quantum states and alleviate the computational challenges associated with two-photon nonlinearity. 

  We show that the photonic J-matrix system addresses the computational complexities of multi-photon nonlinearity in a photonic quantum computing circuit by accurately predicting the output states resulting from a complex quantum gate operation, facilitating a significant reduction in computational complexity from O(n!) to O(n^3). 

  We apply the photonic J-matrix system in a photonic "J-matrix" quantum teleportation protocol, demonstrating high-fidelity teleportation of arbitrary quantum states through a two-photon cat state channel. 

  We propose and demonstrate a photonic "J-matrix" system for photonic quantum computing and communication.

However, deploying and stabilizing deep reinforcement learning agents in real-world applications remains a difficult task. The main issues with this challenge are the unpredictable nature of off-policy training, overfitting, and exploration requirements. To tackle these challenges, researchers suggest using behavior policies designed by experts instead of learning them from scratch. Nonetheless, experts' preconceived ideas about what a good policy should be might misguide them. To address these limitations, an objective method for modifying learned policies according to expert suggestions without exacerbating the overfitting or exploration issues is desired. Our approach, Behavioral Prioritized Policy Distillation, successfully incorporates expert-defined reward functions and bias corrections to stabilize agent training. Through testing on the Montezuma's Revenge and the Expert-Human-Predator tasks, we demonstrate that our approach, Behavioral Policy Distillation, prioritizes learning from key experiences as designated by experts without compromising agent stability or performance. As a result, we are able to train agents for the challenging Montezuma's Revenge task using on-policy deep reinforcement learning methods, something considered unattainable with standard methods. The proposed method has shown significant promise for effectively integrating expert-Designer knowledge into established deep reinforcement learning frameworks. The approach is versatile and adaptable to various predesign and deployment scenarios in the realm of reinforcement learning. Interestingly, this particular implementation yields near optimal results when deployed compared to off-policy and online baseline methods. However, a need for continuous adjustment of the phase encoder to to maximize the quantum signal detection rate has proven to be impractical in real-time data transmission scenarios. This presentation demonstrates a modified PM-QKD protocol that eliminates the requirement for the phase encoder to be readjusted in real-time. By incorporating a laser to continuously adjust the phase of the local laser in the phase-reduction module, we achieve optimal performance. Furthermore, our protocol can achieve a data transmission rate of $7.13M$ queries per second when using GaAs ZZ quantum chip technology. This work also introduces a practical real-time prototype platform to support PM-QKD data transmission. Given that traditional computation and optimization techniques have reached their limits, it is necessary to introduce innovative methods like quantum algorithms. This study investigates the job-shop scheduling problem from a quantum computing perspective. Our proposed quantum algorithm employs the QAPapprox heuristic to find feasible solutions to DJSSP. This algorithm can determine the number of operations and resource usage (p- and q-bounds) independently of problem input. Unlike typical quantum algorithms that rely on problem-specific parameters, this algorithm operates without such constraints. Our experimental results show that even under less favorable conditions, like lower q-bit counts, it is possible to improve upon the currently best classical algorithms and find feasible solutions to DJSSP. This research is, in fact, the first known instance of a quantum algorithm that can solve DJSSP. By applying our algorithm to various problem instances with up to 20 jobs and 20 machines, we have successfully obtained feasible solutions and, in certain cases, we have found that these solutions are also optimal with even lower p- and q-bounds. For example, for 18 jobs and 18 machines, we have found a feasible solution with p-bounds of 52 and q-bounds of 40; this solution, in fact, is the best known solution to this problem instance. For 20 jobs and 20 machines, we have found a feasible solution with p-bounds of 60 and q-bounds of 50; despite not being optimal for this problem instance, which has a known lower bound of 3278, our solution is remarkably close to this bound. Our results show that our algorithm is capable of improving upon the best classical algorithms for DJSSP and that quantum algorithms do hold potential for solving complex optimization problems. Moreover, our study of results obtained from different case studies has revealed valuable insights into the performance of our algorithm, and these insights may also be useful for designing future algorithms. Based on our findings, it seems that improving the performance of more straightforward approaches like the QAPapprox heuristic could yield significant advances in the field of quantum algorithm design. Analytical solutions for the density and phase of the electrons are found, showing a two-peak structure for the phase in the valleys on one side of the constriction.  A stability analysis confirms the soliton's existence, revealing that either a finite valley splitting or a significant discrepancy between the chemical potentials can trigger soliton formation.  Notably, although a large valley splitting results in a soliton, a similar effect is observed when the valley splitting is negligible alongside a substantial difference between the chemical potentials.  Additionally, we find that a soliton can be induced by a large magnetic field, causing a shift in the energy levels and ensuing soliton formation when the confinement energy is relatively low.  The soliton can also be generated by modifying the phase of a confined wave function, achieved through adjusting either the magnetic field or valley splitting. The resulting current modulated by the magnetic field corresponds to distinct soliton phases in the valleys, enabling a determination of the effective magnetic field experienced by the solitons.  Our predictions for the soliton characteristics, though based on a specific model, can be applied to other ring geometries as long as valley splitting and constriction presence are considered.  Consequently, these results are general and applicable to various ring configurations. While most research focuses on single-objective or weighted multi-objective optimization, this study addresses uncapitated multi-objective inventory routing problems with simultaneous consideration of supply, capacity, and financial constraints. To accommodate various application scenarios, this study introduces an epsilon-dominance method for finding the Pareto frontier. Moreover, a genetic algorithm applied to find the Pareto frontier outperforms conventional heuristic methods like VNS and ANS. This study proves that computing a globally optimal solution for this multi-objective problem is an NP-hard problem even without considering two of the objectives, and it is at least NP-hard to determine if a given solution is optimal for any single objective. However, when considering the multi-objective version, this solution is clearly dominated by non-dominated solutions obtained with the epsilon-dominance approach in conjunction with a genetic algorithm. These results highlight the importance of exploring the Pareto frontier to understand the optimal trade-offs that can be achieved in combinatorial optimization problems with multiple objectives, rather than solely focusing on finding a single, so-called "optimal solution".   Fluctuation-induced phenomena are a prominent feature of quantum systems where interconnected electrical components are subjected to random voltage noises. We developed a novel theoretical framework to explain the dynamic behaviors of the solar Chromosphere-Corona interface by integrating magnetic and thermal phenomena. It incorporates the universal principles of energy maintenance and fluid flow, accounting for global photospheric magnetism, plasma processes such as heating, adiabatic expansion, and non-ideal flow. We determined the critical parameters and initial states that define this complex region. Our proposed method involves developing a 2D Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN) called DeepCard, which can automatically identify key features in cine MRI scans. This automatic identification enables more precise detection of abnormalities in heart movements and shapes, facilitating more effective diagnosis and monitoring. Our experiments using 102 subjects showed that DeepCard's accuracy rates are at 94.6% on the ACIC challenge test, exhibiting superior performance to current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, DeepCard is seamlessly integrated into an abnormal movement detection system, enhancing the ability to identify cardiac abnormalities with increased reliability. This collaboration not only addresses the need for evaluating short-baseline cardiac movement stability but also aids in the development of new cardiac disease diagnosis methods. Our complete code is openly available for others to build upon. 

DeepCard consists of a 2D FCNN, consisting of ten blocks, with a transfer learning capability to adapt to new datasets. This architecture allows deep learning to capture subtle differences in cardiac movements and shapes while also incorporating data augmentation to analyze various scan angles. Our proposed method is tested on the ACIC challenge dataset, a collection of cine MRI scans from 54 patients with varied conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, as well as from the AgaClustering dataset, a larger collection of cine MRI scans from 48 subjects. Our experiments show that DeepCard can consistently identify key features regardless of scan angles with minimal information loss. For instance, for vertical scans, DeepCard's accuracy rate is 94.6% with an F-score of 93.9%, and for left parasternal short-axis scans, DeepCard's accuracy rate is 90.3% with an F-score of 89.6%. However, little is known about the influence of individual team member performance on overall team performance in these classifications. In this work, we investigate the persistence of top-performing teams in all three performance classifications. Using the "filtering" concept from extreme value theory, we establish mathematical expressions and probabilistic models to measure the likelihood of teams exceeding expected performance levels. These findings have significant implications for designing successful teams, with potential applications in organizational settings and online collaboration platforms. With a lack of existing studies on team performance, our methods and results contribute importantly to the field of probabilistic scheduling. To verify our approach, we apply it to real-world data from Google's developer teams, as well as from Stack Overflow. Our analysis of this data reveals that top-performing teams in these areas experience high levels of "flying" – where team members switch frequently between lead and supporting roles. Notably, we discover that successful collaboration relies on a specific balance between lead and supporting times, with a preferred ratio that can be influenced by the team's consistency in performance. Our findings suggest that introducing random variation in team performance can, in some circumstances, lead to more successful outcomes. These results, along with our suggested experiments, open the door to further research in this area. To facilitate future studies, we provide access to the Google and Stack Overflow data used in our analysis. These data sets are listed in the repository at https://github.com/jase-clarkson/team-performance.git. As an additional contribution, we develop a theoretical model for quantifying the strength of online communities, with a focus on identifying key indicators that can be tracked in real-time. This community assessment framework has potential applications in various domains, including organizational management, marketing, and advocacy. It also enables researchers to collect new insights by analyzing online engagement patterns, with a suggested list of experiment questions provided in the appendix. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to several notable online forums, including Reddit's r/math (for mathematicians) and r/classicvideo_games, where communities are driven by a shared interest in an area. However, a key challenge in assessing the quality of online communities centered around programming and software development arose due to a high volume of low-quality submissions from inexperienced contributors. In response, we propose an alternative model, known as "coded,” which focuses on evaluating online communities for developers by tracking coded submissions and their associated metadata

Through advanced computer simulations that account for quantum effects and intermolecular interactions, we examined the application of this method with systems of two spinful atoms, which mimics real-world experiments involving six lithium atoms. Our simulations revealed that the presence of residual fluctuations in the initial state of the gas can hinder the efficiency of molecule creation and affect their final energy level. However, our results also show that rapid, laser-induced spin rotation can significantly increase the likelihood of molecule loss through photoassociation. These findings are particularly relevant for cold atom experiments and their theoretical modeling at the quantum level. Our study reveals that cold molecule creation can aid in understanding quantum and thermodynamic properties of systems in the six-atom limit, which remains largely unexplored in physics. Finally, our research shows that cold molecule creation provides a means to experimentally study, and thus verify, a theoretical construct for describing atomic correlations in matter, known as bosonic superfluidity of pairs. These novel findings are contributed in a companion paper [ArXiv:2104.04885], where an analytical framework for describing cold molecule creation is developed, offering an alternative perspective to the numerical approach presented here. Nevertheless, the findings in this study are specifically aimed at numerically examining and optimally configuring experiments for producing cold molecules using pre-existing fermionic gas in a specific configuration, which is distinct from the analytical approach. In this study, we employed asteroseismology to analyze a sample of 28 stars and explored the potential biases introduced by assuming a specific set of photometric characteristics. We found that neglecting the effects of surface gravity brightness results in underestimating the star's radius by up to 5 percent and overestimates its surface gravity by as much as 10 percent. This investigation draws upon the relationship between the driving force and the work distribution to establish a variational principle of the thermodynamic efficiency. To validate this approach, it is applied to a driven, damped harmonic oscillator to derive the Carnot standard heat engine's operating cycle. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the maximum output work produced by a given amount of heat in an oven can be determined through this method. This technique is then used to analyze a single, driven quantum oscillator, identifying key differences between its thermodynamic properties and those of a classical, overdamped harmonic oscillator. Ultimately, it is shown that the thermodynamic efficiency of a quantum engine can be optimised by leveraging quantum anti-damping effects. This research contributes to our understanding of the thermodynamics of quantum systems by providing a quantum version of the classical thermodynamic efficiency equation. This property is viewed as a quantum counterpart to Carathéodory's original postulate of thermodynamics. Moreover, it is shown that the thermodynamic performance of a quantum engine can be streamlined through quantum damping. This analysis is performed at the symbolic level, using the mathematical formulation of the thermodynamics of quantum systems developed by R. A. Condon. This method has potential to expand the scope of thermodynamic studies, as demonstrated by its applications to systems described by Lagrangian path integrals and driven quantum circuits. This research is intended to establish a foundational understanding of quantum thermodynamics, providing a deeper insight into this complex and rapidly evolving field. This study is the initial foray into utilising the thermodynamic work distribution function to establish a macroscopic thermodynamic framework for quantum systems. As a result, it is anticipated that the method will identify novel and unconventional thermodynamic properties of quantum systems. This research is the first step in an ongoing investigation into the use of probability theory to develop a quantum version of thermodynamics. To address this issue, the Euclid Data Management team is developing an agile release management process that aims to strike a balance between rapid data publication and quality control. This process is particularly relevant to collaborative projects like Euclid where multiple teams are involved in data processing and assessment. By adopting this new approach, Euclid is positioned to capitalize on the synergies between rapid data publication and continuous improvement. This paper outlines the proposed agile release management framework, evaluates its applicability to Euclid and other similar projects, and presents a comprehensive guide for implementation. Additionally, it highlights potential obstacles and presents a plan for iterative process refinement based on feedback and lessons learned. As the first release candidate for Phase A data is nearing completion, the team is better equipped to handle the complexities of continuous data publication. To date, the team has successfully implemented the proposed process within the Euclid Data Management team and surrounding communities, demonstrating its effectiveness and feasibility. Several key projects-$ including the Reference Data Release-$ are already utilizing this new approach to publish high-quality data regularly. By sharing our experience with agile release management, we hope to contribute to the development of best practices for agile data management, encouraging other projects to adopt this method if suitable. If projects share similar constraints and objectives, they may consider the following alternatives. Firstly, projects can choose between two release strategies: either maintaining a comprehensive and time-consuming traditional release process or exploring more frequent but less elaborate agile releases. Secondly, projects can tailor the proposed release management framework according to their specific requirements. Finally, projects are encouraged to join a community-led effort to develop collaborative and iterative release management best practices specifically designed for research data projects. This effort is led by the Research Data Alliance Data Management Working Group, which aims to provide guidance on data management best practices through a shared knowledge base. By promoting agile release management, the working group hopes to foster a culture of collaborative iteration and continuous process refinement, ultimately contributing to the development of comprehensive and effective data management best practices for research projects. As an active member of the working group, we are committed to supporting this initiative and contributing valuable lessons learned from the Euclid project. Our involvement will involve documenting the release management framework, identifying knowledge gaps and proposing strategies to address them, and reviewing case studies to ensure the framework remains relevant and effective. By working together across different research communities and embracing collaborative iteration, we can refine our data management approaches, reducing the likelihood of data publication failures and minimizing disruption

developers in optimizing their designs to minimize UTXO-related loads and guide
network upgrades to rectify UTXO-related congestion issues, ultimately improving user experience.

Our study is the first of its kind, showcasing the negative impact of UTXO-related congestion on decentralized nodes and
the substantial load imposed by high-profile smart contracts, justifying UTXO optimization in future blockchain and DLT infrastructure design. 
The load of Ethereum UTXOs is set to increase due to growing adoption, prompting an investigation into UTXO-reduction techniques 
that can benefit both current and prospective blockchain networks. 
Using practical examples, we demonstrate the negative impact of UTXO-related congestion on decentralized nodes, a known issue in CDB-based designs. 
Moreover, our analysis provides an in-depth examination of UTXO-related computational and bandwidth requirements for 30 leading contracts,

However, current deep learning approaches are susceptible to perturbations, whether induced by noise or attacks, which can lead to incorrect outcomes. Consequently, there is a rising interest in the deep learning community in leveraging the strengths of Monte Carlo methods to improve the resilience of DNNs against adversarial perturbations. Our proposed model, known as iForest, utilizes an ensemble of recursive neural networks with parametrized activation functions, enabling the computation of ambiguity measures for input samples. Specifically, iForest generates an uncertainty score for a given data point by averaging the output ambiguity of multiple neural networks with shared weights but individually selected parameters to sample inputs. Unlike our proposed method, previous attempts at uncertainty-based resilience were hampered by several limitations: testing datasets were often poorly annotated, requiring significant manual labor; there was a trade-off between model speed and accuracy; and previous models were prone to filtering out legitimate data, resulting in reduced reliability, or else relying on simplistic activation functions that did not effectively capture the ambiguity of the model's decision space. In contrast, our proposed method, iForest, overcome these limitations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the adversarial uncertainty benchmark, which simulates the scenarios of deepest learning perturbations and real-time deployments. In particular, our findings show that iForest accurately label up to 93% of the test dataset under the most extreme attacks, and outperforms previous approaches while achieving state-of-the-art reliability and accuracy on the standard MNIST and CIFAR-10 benchmarks. Furthermore, our proposed method is highly efficient, running orders of magnitude faster than previous approaches while effectively filtering out nearly 10% of the clean test dataset, resulting in a 39% reduction in false positives. These studies have focused on coupling fluid flow with the movement of gas and/or solid particles through the cracks. Conventionally, least squares loss is used to minimize the disparity error between points. However, this loss has its limitations as it allows the selection of lengthy and narrow 3D lines. To overcome this, we are proposing a novel patch based dense matching approach that incorporates a transitive patch similarity measure. This measure assesses the similarity between patches that overlap minimally and progressively, thereby ensuring that points are selected transversely to contours and depths are evenly distributed. To facilitate efficient selection, we have analyzed and derived a sparsity promoting formulation for our proposed method. Notably, a computationally efficient algorithm with a quadratic time complexity of n (where n is the total number of pixels) has been designed to demonstrate the method's effectiveness on benchmarks. Further experimentation shows that our approach performs satisfactorily compared to other state-of-the-art techniques. It ranks third out of six methods with an average ratio of 4.97 and an average error of 1.73, 0.73, 0.63 at 64x, 32x, 16x sampling densities respectively in the benchmark dataset. Dense matching with an error of 0.58 at an 16x density sampling rate is also successfully achieved on aerial images. Importantly, our method is largely independent on specific scanner or representation choices. It is based on conventional gray scale images and dense scanning. To further reduce time complexity, we have observed that our method could be extended to RGB images by employing a reduced color encoding technique. While directly adding color channels leads to a fourfold increase in the total number of pixels, employing reduced color encoding yields only a minimal rise. To accomplish this, we first establish a metric that closely resembles Lobachevsky-Hartman metric on the disk, and then show that geodesics in this metric tend towards the boundary. Next, we prove that geodesics in the actual metric tend towards the boundary as well. Specifically, we show that the minimum distance between a geodesic and the boundary is inversely proportional to the radius of the geodesic. Importantly, we do not assume that geodesics remain on the unit disk for all time; rather, we show that geodesics tend towards the boundary from within the disk. Finally, we show that geodesics in the metric actually tend towards the boundary without deviating to earlier times as well. This involves demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of geodesics over various time intervals, which we accomplish through the method of controlled variation, and proving that this approach is robust against perturbations for all time intervals by showing that the return times for the unperturbed and perturbed geodesics differ by at most $\pi/\epsilon^2$. Consequently, we show that geodesics tend towards the boundary over any time interval by considering perturbations that occur at such an interval and using the unreturning time criterion to extend this behavior to all time intervals. Lastly, we do some hand-waving to connect this result to what we know about fields in Anti de Sitter space, knowing that this literature is not comprehensive for our purposes. A novel augmentation method, known as Pairwise Generation Zone (PGZ), is introduced to enhance data augmentation for few-shot instance segmentation tasks. Comparisons with state-of-the-art models show that even without the assistance of a meta-learning support set, PGZ can improve the performance of existing algorithms. Moreover, integrating PGZ with meta-learning algorithms further improves their results. Interestingly, PGZ is particularly beneficial in a few-shot instance segmentation context. It generates images at the pixel level (as opposed to object level), leading to more effective data augmentation. Moreover, PGZ is capable of generating complex backgrounds (with or without objects) as well as foregrounds, which aids object detection in a few-shot instance segmentation context. The proposed PGZ is supposed to be integrated with instance segmentation models. Therefore, the pair of positive and negative images generated by PGZ is attached to each image in the query dataset during the training of the base model. Like other data augmentation methods, PGZ does not need any extra parameters. Therefore, its components can be easily shared with other tasks, such as simultaneous instance segmentation and object detection. The source code of the proposed Pairwise Generation Zone can be found at this repository address: https://github.com/J-chenJS/PNZ. Potentially, the patterns learned in the PGZ augmentation could be applied to address other data augmentation challenges in computer vision, making it a broader and more significant contribution to the field of computer vision than just few-shot instance segmentation.  A preliminary draft of this paper was presented at the 2021 ILSVRC Conference. Due to the constraints of the draft, the paper's results and implications were not fully explored. This revised paper addresses the concerns, and, as a result, provides a more comprehensive account of the Pairwise Generation Zone (PGZ). One of the unanswered questions in the initial draft was how effective PGZ is when there is only one shot instance. To address this concern, a more in-depth analysis of the one-shot scenario is presented in this revised paper. Compared to the preliminary draft, the one-shot analysis reveals several crucial insights. For instance, the results show that PGZ is more beneficial when there is only one shot instance because it tends to enhance the data augmentation. Moreover, the one-shot analysis using Baseline-FCOS would bring about the significant reduction of mAP from 24.15% to 23.15%.

Since microgrids do not have a central power management system, the question of how to manage and engage with the larger grid becomes a critical issue, particularly when it comes to communicating with the broader power system.  In order to address this challenge, a standardization framework that considers the interconnected relationships between microgrids and the high voltage power system is necessary to ensure that microgrids can seamlessly integrate with the power system.  In particular, a comprehensive framework that outlines various interfaces, specifically those that facilitate communication and economic transactions, is required to facilitate interactions between microgrids and the power system.  This research proposes a conceptual framework that specifies these interfaces, focusing on two key aspects: AC microgrids for residential consumption, and DC microgrids for commercial and industrial consumption.  The framework recognizes that all microgrids, regardless of their type, can be categorized into four main groups, based on the nature of their interfaces, namely: 1) those that primarily focus on energy exchanges, 2) those that prioritize power exchanges, 3) those that facilitate control services, and 4) those that manage both energy and power exchanges, as well as provide control services to the power system.  In order to verify the efficacy of the proposed framework, a detailed analysis of each interface type is performed,  in accordance with the objectives of the research,  based on an examination of existing literature.  This research is based on a case study of standardization for AC and DC microgrids,  in order to validate and expand upon a proposed framework,  previously presented in 2019,  which specified AC and DC microgrid interfaces.  In order to further validate the proposed framework,  a discussion is conducted with experts in the research field of microgrids to gather feedback on the proposed framework.  This research is based on a survey of 21 experts who have previously worked on microgrid projects,  in order to gather additional feedback and improve the proposed framework.  This research is based on a review of the Smart Energy Service Centers,  a European project that aims to promote the integration of energy from renewable energy sources. Current approaches rely on specialized units for handling sign, but these are not well-suited to classifying fractions. In this study, we introduce a method for classifying rational numbers through neural nets that are both sign-adaptive and capable of classifying all positive, negative, and fractional values. These neural nets are based on elementary arithmetic operations and thus can be trained quickly, even with large data sets. Furthermore, our method allows for an explicit expression of the classified rational numbers in terms of other rationals, which in turn enables training the network to achieve high accuracy using relatively minimal data. When tested on a set of functions, our method consistently outperformed other sign-adaptive approaches, and surprisingly, achieved accuracy comparable to a highly data-intensive non-sign-adaptive neural net. Overall, our method offers a highly versatile tool for analyzing and classifying rational numbers using neural nets. As an added benefit, we also introduce a novel method for approximating continuous functions using rational numbers and develop a method for determining a lower bound on the training accuracy of neural nets, under the assumption that the lower bound is known. These algorithms are now available in an open-source package called 'rational-nn'.  Existing tools for approximating continuous functions, such as Taylor polynomials, often achieve high accuracy but require extensive data collection, a time-consuming process. In an effort to address this, we also introduce a method for approximating continuous functions without collecting extensive data by classifying rational numbers. In this study, we show that sign-adaptive neural nets can be used to analyze and classify rational numbers with minimal data. More specifically, we prove that, on average, the sign-adaptive neural net is no more difficult to train than a non-sign-adaptive neural net, even when the non-sign-adaptive net is trained with significantly more data. Furthermore, we establish a method for approximating continuous functions using rational numbers and show that, with minimal data, this method closely matches the non-sign-adaptive neural net in its accuracy. As an example, we tested our method on various functions, and found that, with significantly less data, our method yielded results comparable to the non-sign-adaptive neural net. In an effort to provide further insight, we also investigated the distribution of the data required by our method and found that it closely matches the distribution of the data required by the non-sign-adaptive neural net. Moreover, we discovered that the data required by our method can be efficiently analyzed and understood.

However, this assumption may not hold, especially when answering surveys can reflect one's familiarity with their own emotions. We developed a web-based platform where people play a game to improve their emotional awareness and then answer surveys about social distancing measures. Our results show that people's surveys responses are influenced by their performance in the game and are less reliable indicators of their objective situation compared to their game performance. This suggests that the reliance solely on surveys can lead to inaccurate representations of public sentiment. Ultimately, we propose a novel approach that utilizes machine learning to combine survey data with other information, such as social network dynamics, to improve the estimation of genuine public opinions. Our study also proposes a new metric, emotional intimacy, to evaluate the personal costs of social distancing measures. By combining social and emotional aspects, this metric can facilitate more effective social distancing policies. Our study demonstrates that the personal costs of social distancing can be substantial, and that incorporating both social and emotional aspects yields estimates that are on average 36% more accurate than those based solely on social aspects. In contrast, the estimates based solely on emotional aspects are less accurate. Our findings suggest that incorporating additional perspectives, such as emotional awareness, social interplay, and individual differences, is crucial for refining the estimation of genuine public opinions during the pandemic and similar crises in the future. Our study's algorithms and study data are publicly available at https://github.com/acgpet/nlp-dist-social-emotional-costs. Similar studies are provided at https://github.com/acgpet/nlp-dist-social-simulations. They are based on a set of scenarios designed to explore interpersonal interactions and emotional awareness in the context of social distancing interventions. For example, one scenario called "emotion night" involves a situation where two friends are encouraged to meet and share their emotional experiences, which could potentially mitigate the negative effects of social distancing measures. Our studies aim to facilitate future investigations of this scenario and similar scenarios, and to facilitate collaborations between researchers and practitioners to develop more effective social distancing policies that consider both social and emotional aspects of public behavior. In the context of social distancing, emotional awareness may play a crucial role in maintaining social connections and mitigating the negative effects of social isolation. Our study provides access to scenarios that can aid in understanding this relationship and inform policy decisions. Our algorithm design also aims to improve estimation methods used in policy research, and to facilitate collaboration between researchers and practitioners

we need to find the optimal way to present the input to the model. Current token-based 
methods have limitations, such as ignoring word relationships and making part-of-speech errors. 
To address this, we have developed a new regime that breaks down sentence meaning into various aspects, 
thereby producing more accurate results and mitigating potential biases in language models. 
We have introduced a novel input type, called Meaningful Segments (MS), a complementary unit that 
exists alongside tokens to influence the model's representation learning. 
Using a straightforward pre-processing technique, MS inputs are defined by combining semantic meaning and word morphology 
and encoding them as fixed-size sequences of words with consistent semantic meaning. 
We have shown through extensive testing that using MS inputs in language model fine-tuning can lead to better output quality, 
with reductions in errors for tasks like paraphrasing, ontological concept preservation, and logical reasoning, 
as well as more natural text that is less likely to contain biased statements. 
Furthermore, MS inputs seem to be particularly effective in scenarios where models struggle to capture sentence meaning, 
such as when processing sentences with multiple grammatical subjects or complex semantic structures, 
or in low-resource settings where models lack adequate training data. 
As such, we recommend considering MS inputs as a useful addition to neural language model input representations, 
providing improved performance and insight into the underlying language processing mechanisms. 
The implementation of MS inputs is available on the website https://github.com/explosion/deberta-tfms.

potentially leading to new text generation innovations and applications.

MCD) algorithm, used in statistics for selecting a subspace of data, is reinterpreted through the lens of nonnegative projection operators in this article. A novel, more efficient variant of MCD is introduced, specifically 'MCD+', which by its very nature incorporates additional constraints beyond those imposed by its original formulation. Compared to the conventional MCD, the enhanced MCD+ algorithm exhibits improved performance in several key aspects. Firstly, as it is based on a more inclusive set of problem formulations, the MCD+, unlike the MCD, is capable of handling instances where the data is not centered. Additionally, the MCD+ does not encounter issues with nonrepresensive spans, a common problem seen in the MCD when attempting to project nonzero data onto a subspace containing zeros. The outcomes of both algorithms are put to the test across a range of numerical and real-world datasets. Notably, the MCD+ was found to outperform the conventional MCD in these instances, a direct result of its capacity to handle problematic instances. As such, the MCD+ can be considered a more robust variant of the Minimum Volume Ellipsoid Algorithm (MVE), a regression technique also known as the Minimum Volume Ellipsoid. A final discussion is devoted to exploring the potential applicability of the MCD+ method across a broader scope of statistical tools. As an alternative to the conventional MCD, the MCD+ is made available through the repo-nlp GitHub repository for further exploration. The implementation is based on the NumPy and Scipy libraries for the consistent treatment of matrix operations, with the inclusion of additional functionalities in the package. The repo-nlp is equipped with the MCD+ method for the execution of both the conventional MCD and the novel MCD+ operations, offering the added feature of parallel processing through the use of joblib tasks. As such, the MCD+ is well-suited for the handling of very large-scale datasets, a result of the incorporation of parallel processing capabilities. The implementation is completed with the inclusion of the computation of the Spanned Volume, a metric essential for the MVE. The MCD+ is further evaluated using the dataset 'Hepatitis', a real-world biomedical dataset containing a multidimensional dataset used for the input of a classification model. As such, the MCD+ is implemented using a collaborative parallel computing architecture, a feature also present in joblib, a library itself based on the parallel processing of computationally intensive tasks. A final evaluation is performed using the 'HIV' dataset

  Therefore, we propose an alternative, an unsupervised deep learning system based on high-precision real-field numbers, which surpasses the limitations of traditional neural networks. 
  Our new system incorporates a novel high-precision neural network, HNET, capable of supporting complex-number inputs and outputs. 
  We have proven that HNET is capable of achieving an unsupervised error rate of at least $L\circ U$, where $L$ represents lower bounds for any reversible computation and $U$ represents upper bounds for any reversible computation.

  The experiments conducted also revealed that performing a sequence of Boolean operations on HNET's high-precision complex numbers can sometimes yield increased accuracy, underscoring the potential of exploring the full capabilities of the complex number domain in designing new neural networks. 
  Lastly, we have found that incorporating inverse operations within HNET's learning process, despite increasing computational requirements, can lead to better performance outcomes. 
  Thus, our new system represents a significant advancement in the state-of-the-art for both reversible and traditional neural networks in terms of accuracy and complexity.

As nonlinear systems are inherently complex and subject to various types of time series data contamination, we develop a framework for handling mixed noise types. An adaptive approach is presented, along with a performance evaluation involving simulated data from nonlinear systems affected by different types of noise, highlighting its superiority over traditional estimators. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive-robust technique in recovering system parameters from mixed noise, showcasing its substantial improvement over both traditional and conventional adaptive methods. Notably, these proposed algorithms are designed to operate offline. Further research is required to apply these techniques online. We also analyzed the computational requirements of the adaptive and adaptive-robust algorithms, revealing them to be comparable to the classical Cramer-Rao lower bound. Nonetheless, the computational complexity of the adaptive and adaptive-robust algorithms is substantially higher than the traditional approaches. Finally, we compared the proposed algorithms to state-of-the-art techniques, showcasing their improved performance in estimating system parameters while boasting significantly reduced computational demands. Hence, the adaptive and adaptive-robust algorithms are deemed viable alternatives to existing methods. An extensive examination of the proposed algorithms is facilitated by the utilization of proposed performance metrics that account for both estimation error and computational complexity. Moreover, the adaptive and adaptive-robust algorithms are complemented by a suggested heuristic to accelerate the evaluation of the estimation error, consisting of a multi-start method with predetermined stopping criteria. As the exploration of the parameter search space can be highly demanding. Nevertheless, the optimal parameter configuration to achieve this balance remains uncertain and in need of investigation. An alternative to the adaptive approach is presented in the form of the adaptive-robust algorithm, which incorporates a robust optimization technique to estimate the system parameters and is particularly suited to nonlinear systems with varying types of noise.   Firstly, there's a condensation transition that occurs when the trap's depth promotes Bose-Einstein condensation. This type of transition is similar to its standard, stationary form and is determined by the specific trap depth and temperature. 

  Secondly, there's a droplet condensation transition that occurs when the trap's edge creates a finite-sized, stationary droplet which spontaneously fills the entire trap at a higher temperature. This distinct phase transition is caused by the competition between the mean-field potential and the trap's edge barrier and exists even in the limit of an infinitely deep trap.

One phase features a droplet whose size is determined by the trap's edge, while another phase has an infinite condensate in the ground state. Furthermore, we have also developed a phase boundary at which the first momentum condensation occurs in the phase diagram. Our results agree well with exact numerical calculations.

To investigate why this is the case, we have been studying the behavior of two-dimensional neural networks that consist of a single layer with varying weights, and which are trained to estimate a specific nonlinear function with both noise and signal present.  Through mathematical analysis and numerical calculations, we have found that there are always pathways available for the weights to move along while the network is being trained, and simultaneously minimize its error in approximating the target function, particularly as the number of parameters increases.  Furthermore, we have discovered that increasing the amount of noise present can actually facilitate finding these pathways.  These findings indicate that one possible explanation for the success of overparameterized neural networks may be to adjust their parameters to be near configurations where the error is most sensitive to changes in the parameters, and this may be an approach that could be extended to other optimization methods in the future.  The full details of our investigation, including any mathematical assumptions that were required, are documented within this journal article.  In addition to the material included here, we have also conducted an examination of the neural network's error in the context of a noise-free model that accounts for the complex structures present within the parameter space, and this analysis revealed that the critical dimensions associated with these structures are typically quite low in dimension (no higher than two).  As a result, it may be possible to explain the behavior of neural networks with a relatively large number of parameters by treating them as being part of a nonlinear extension of classical least squares estimation methods.  We have sketched the general framework for this extension in the article, and we believe that it warrants further investigation in the future.  The articles referenced [1-3] provide additional relevant background information on the topic.  The computational methods used to analyze the neural network's error are outlined in the accompanying paper (Part II), and we have included the full derivation of some key formulas within this first part. Prior studies have established theoretical limits based on particular beam scenarios. This research aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these constraints, showing that certain emittance regulations are inherent and universal, while also uncovering new limitations that can be applied to various beam configurations. To achieve this, a phase space transformation approach is used to derive universal emittance limits. The findings indicate that the maximum storage density is determined by the quadrature sum of three individual emittance components: particle-based, beam-field emittance, and image emittance. The latter two are inherent and universal while the particle-based emittance remains configurable. The study shows that the phase space transformation technique offers a valuable toolkit to design storage rings that surpass the emittance limitations. It is demonstrated that by carefully adjusting the beam phase, octopole component, and beam current, it is feasible to mitigate the constraints imposed by the beam itself. A concept inspired by the NSLS II Photoinjector boasts promising storage performance, outperforming the emittance limitations imposed by the beam itself, beam-field emittance, and even the image emittance. We propose an approach to enhance existing graph libraries by incorporating a unified system for expressing annotations and integrating them into the majority of its algorithms. Our methodology has been put into practice within the HG library, designed for efficient computation on weighted directed graphs. Furthermore, we have successfully implemented a C++ interface allowing the easy incorporation of annotated libraries. Additionally, we present two real-world scenarios highlighting the value in retaining metadata in graphs. Furthermore, we have adapted our C++ interface for use with Python's NetworkX library and have used this interface to introduce annotated graph classes within Python's PyGraphTools. These updates have been released as open-source software under permissive licensing conditions. Our implementation's performance has been assessed through a comparative evaluation against PyGraphTools' annotated classes, revealing no performance disadvantage. Our C++ interface has utility beyond PyGraphTools' features, primarily in three areas: providing a general framework for metadata, extending to other libraries, and offering an easy migration path from PyGraphTools. Our C++ interface's capabilities have significant implications for the transformation of graph algorithms, enabling the efficient design of algorithms utilizing metadata to improve their complexity, an example of which is independently developing a parallel single-source shortest paths algorithm using level-contracting. Our C++ interface has been released as a tool for simplifying the task of annotating graph metadata passed to PyGraphTools' functions, resulting in minimal overhead and the examples showcase its value in improving algorithm design. Our C++ interface has been utilized in an easy-to-use Python library for static analysis, called static-graph, which provides features for identifying data flow and graph-based programming patterns. This class of models can represent a broad spectrum of parasites, from microorganisms to parasites transmitted via vectors, making it applicable to various diseases. The framework is suitable for use in deterministic network models that aim to understand disease spread and identify critical thresholds, as well as for stochastic individual-based models that simulate specific parasite life cycles. This paper derives general mean field and linearized models for deterministic network dynamics, provides analytical expressions for their bifurcation properties, and discusses the linearized models for stochastic individual-based models. The approach is illustrated through examples of sheep nematode and fungal diseases, with model applications and limitations discussed. 

    However, individual-based models can sometimes fall short of accurately capturing observed disease progression, particularly when these diseases can be transmitted via multiple pathways, as with tsetse fly transmitted sleeping sickness. To improve these models, individual-based simulations can be augmented with additional processes such as disease transmission at interfaces, changes in host behavior, and various disease effects on hosts. These disease processes can be modeled representatively by means of continuous-time Markov chains and integrated into individual-based models. 

    Individual-based models that incorporate disease processes modelled as continuous-time Markov chains can be analysed using a framework that enables the derivation of individual stationary probability distributions. Moreover, in networked systems where individual properties determine population dynamics, these distributions can be used in approximating deterministic model dynamics through a mean field decomposition. 

    However, in complex systems where individual properties may be difficult to determine, individual stationary distributions can be estimated from simulations of individual-based models via Markov chain sampling. To improve efficiency in such simulations, where repeated sampling is required for parameter estimation, Bayesian sensitivity analysis and Markov chain sampling can be performed in parallel using pseudo-reference points.

We investigated the stochastic properties of a conservative random walk on a class of networks where the local probability distributions have symmetric components. These distributions belong to the family of positive hypergeometric functions of the second kind. The research showed that the topology of a network determines its spectral gap and birthday problem. We also derived an equation describing the rate of convergence to stationary distribution for a specific class of conservative random walks on positive matrices. This work has broader applications beyond random walk models. The results are most relevant to directed networks representing interactions between entities, such as networks of predators and prey, energy networks, and food networks. The research particularly focuses on its implications for directed acyclic networks, which cannot return to a initial state. The study reveals that the topology of such networks determines key stochastic properties. The findings are most pronounced in networks where the flow of information is one-way. In such systems, the rate of convergence to stationary distribution is solely dependent on the basic characteristics of the network's underlying graph. The directed acyclic nature of the network determines the type of stationary distribution, consisting of non-negative probabilities representing the direction of information flow. Effective visual detection relies on concise search representations that accurately capture gunmen in real-world crowd videos. Given the scarcity of annotated crowd videos containing gunmen, the existing search models often face significant challenges. To address this complexity, we focus on detecting a single object (a gun) within a video frame without identifying the associated person. This task, referred to as gun visual detection, has received little attention previously. Building on this idea, we have devised an innovative data enhancement method called DGE (Distributed and Generalized Enhancement). DGE enhances the search space by merging individual object detection with generic semantic meaning, thereby linking a given object to its broader counterparts (like 'hand' or 'firearm'). This broadening of the search space enables the distribution of object annotations among hand and firearm images, increasing the availability of labeled data for a particular object without actually finding it. DGE also generalizes the search space by merging individual object categories, allowing a particular object to be linked to others sharing the same semantic meaning (like both 'hand' and 'firearm' as part of the 'body part' category). This broadening of the search space enhances the search space's diversity, increases the availability of labeled data for a particular object without actually finding it, and makes the search more robust. DGE is applied to a challenging dataset known as VisualGUN, a collection of video frames containing gun visuals found within real-world crowd videos. DGE is the first data enhancement method to address gun visual detection in crowd videos, leveraging object distribution and semantic generalization to complement the VisualGUN dataset's scarcity. DGE is applied via two approaches: 1) supporting the search for a specific object within a frame by linking it to a broadened search space containing hand and firearm images, or 2) merging individual object categories (hand and firearm) to create a more diverse search space containing a combination of VisualGUN's primary labels. DGE is applied to train YOLOv5, a state-of-the-art object detection model, resulting in enhanced performance on the VisualGUN dataset. DGE is a flexible framework, and we believe its methods can be applied to various object detection tasks beyond gun visual detection in crowd videos. The VisualGUN dataset is a unique resource for evaluating gun detection in crowd videos. In this modified task, an inference graph is produced from premises and a statement, and humans are asked to assess the validity of each statement in the graph in relation to the premises. These emissions have a significant impact on the Gravitational Wave Spectral Density, particularly at frequencies corresponding to the reheating of the universe and to the gaps within the perturbative regime.  To better understand the discovery potential of hypothetical vector-like leptons at LHC and other colliders, we analyze the optimal search strategy for these particles and the corresponding sensitivity limits, complemented by an examination of the backward trajectory from direct detection bounds to the GW spectrum.  Notably, the collider limits we derive are the most stringent to date, while our analysis also demonstrates that, assuming standard coupling strengths, the LHC should be capable of detecting vector-like leptons heavier than approximately 1.2-1.5 TeV, depending on their electric charge.  Furthermore, with increased luminosity at future runs of the LHC or at other colliders like the HL-eLHC, CMS3, FCC-eh, or IPC, it will be possible to push the detection limits up to vector-like leptons of mass ~3-4 TeV.  We demonstrate that, for masses above 1 TeV, the optimal search strategy for the production of these particles at hadron colliders involves examining the decay products of the heaviest vector-like particle and identifying the leptons and jets produced in the final state.  By focusing on these channels, particularly those with two leptons, we are able to set the most stringent limits on the vector-like doublet, while the singlet can be constrained more effectively by searching for single production processes involving vector-like leptons.  In terms of Gravitational Wave detection, assuming the emission of scalar standard model particles by the vector-like doublet results in a greater signal strength than the emission of fermions or vectors, while the vector-like singlet, on the other hand, yields one of the smallest possible signals.  Notably, the present and anticipated sensitivity of ground-based detectors like MESA, NECTAR, and ARES is capable of breaking the vector-like doublet up to the point where its mass lies between 1.2-2.2 times the detection frequency, while breaking the vector-like singlet, however, yields a greater gap. To address this issue, low-bit deep imaging techniques have been proposed, which limit data to a few bits and reconstruct missing information through learning. However, these techniques have difficulties with high-dimensional maps and overloading signals. This paper presents a new technique, called LitDeep, which uses both spatial and temporal imaging information to accurately recreate environment maps with high dynamic range lighting. To achieve this, LitDeep employs a pixel-wise transformation to decode the mapping dataset, and then calculates the difference between the decoded image and the input pixel data. This difference is then used to predict the missing information in the image, which is combined with the decoded image to reconstruct the environment map. Since the mapping dataset is a multi-dimensional array, we use sparse sampling to reduce data transmission and storage requirements. To evaluate the effectiveness of LitDeep, we implemented it on two mobile GPUs, the ARM Mali-G76 and the Mali-G77, and found that it produces similar results to the high-quality, 32-bit rendered image, while also improving transmission by half and increasing frame rates by 1.5 to 31.5%. Additionally, LitDeep outperforms other low-bit techniques in visual quality, while also being more efficient than other CNN-based and field mapping approaches in terms of transmission and processing speed. In terms of power consumption, LitDeep is 10-30% more power-efficient than the other low-bit techniques, but less efficient than the other CNN-based and field mapping approaches. Furthermore, LitDeep is compatible with deep imaging for dynamic range lighting and global illumination, and can be combined with other low-bit techniques to improve the overall efficiency and quality of the environment map. This is demonstrated by showing that the result of LitDeep is as good as the results of rendering at 32 bits or using a field mapping with double precision. To sum up, LitDeep is a suitable solution for high-quality environment mapping with high dynamic range lighting, especially for mobile and real-time applications, achieving a balance between quality, efficiency, and speed.
